meta.title: Answer Sense
meta.intro: Every question here comes with a common answer that is scientifically true and still does not score. The point is not the science, which you may already know. The point is the gap between a true statement and an answer that responds to what was asked. Read the question, decide in your head what the answer must contain, then reveal the common answer and the thinking behind why it falls short.

failureTypes.label: Named a keyword, not the mechanism
failureTypes.blurb: The right process is named, but the answer stops there. It is too short: it never says where things came from or what drove the change.

failureTypes.label: Gave the evidence, not the conclusion
failureTypes.blurb: The observation is restated as if it were the answer. An infer or conclude question wants the step from evidence to conclusion.

failureTypes.label: Answered half the question
failureTypes.blurb: A two-part question, or one with a comparison clause, was answered on one side only. Half the marks were left on the table.

failureTypes.label: True but too general
failureTypes.blurb: The statement is correct but generic. It was never tied to this scenario, this animal, this habitat, so it could have been written without reading the question.

failureTypes.label: Restated the question
failureTypes.blurb: The prediction or observation was repeated back with no reason attached. The marks were for the reason, not the restatement.

failureTypes.label: Compared one-sidedly
failureTypes.blurb: A property of one thing was given instead of a contrast between both. A compare answer must set the two against each other.

items.stimulus: Water droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced water left on a table.
items.stem: Explain how the water droplets formed on the outside of the glass.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'name the process that put water on the glass' and reaches for the word condensation.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to trace the water back to its source in the surrounding air and give the reason it turned liquid, not just to label the change.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can build the full condensation mechanism: water vapour in the air, losing heat to the cold glass, changing to liquid.
items.weakAnswer: The water vapour condensed and turned into water droplets on the glass.
items.thinkingGap: He treated 'explain how it formed' as 'name the process', so he wrote the label and stopped. A formation question has three hidden parts: where the water came from (water vapour already in the surrounding air, not water seeping through the glass), what drove the change (the vapour touched the cold surface and lost heat energy to it), and the result (it condensed into liquid). His sentence gives only the result. 'Condensed' is the conclusion of the mechanism, not the mechanism itself, so at two marks he earns at most one.
items.strongAnswer: Water vapour in the surrounding air came into contact with the cold surface of the glass. The water vapour lost heat energy to the colder glass and condensed, changing from the gaseous state into liquid water. This formed droplets on the outside of the glass.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the source (vapour in the air), the driver (loses heat to the colder glass) and the change (condenses to liquid), so it lands both marks: the heat-loss step and the change of state.
items.attentionCue: Explain how it formed = it came FROM somewhere + something MADE it happen + the result. Naming the result is only the last third.

items.stimulus: Two identical dishes hold 50 ml of water each. Dish A is left in a shaded corner. Dish B is left beside a sunny window. Both are checked after four hours.
items.stem: Predict which dish will contain less water after four hours, explain your answer, and state one thing that must be kept the same for this to be a fair test.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'which dish loses more water and why', answers that well, and treats the fair-test line as decoration.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for three separate things: the prediction, the reason, and one variable that must be kept the same to make it a fair test.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he notices that the stem has a third, separately marked demand, the control variable, tacked on after 'explain your answer'.
items.weakAnswer: Dish B will contain less water, because it receives more heat energy from the sun, so its rate of evaporation is higher and more water evaporates.
items.thinkingGap: Everything he wrote is correct and would earn the first two marks, which is exactly why the slip is invisible to him. The stem is really three instructions joined by commas: predict, explain, and 'state one thing that must be kept the same'. Once he had a satisfying prediction and reason, his brain marked the question done and skated over the final clause. The fair-test mark is the easiest in the question, name the starting volume or the size of the dish, but you only score it if you notice it is being asked. At three marks, missing it throws away a third of the answer.
items.strongAnswer: Dish B will contain less water. Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight than Dish A, and the greater the heat energy gained, the higher the rate of evaporation, so more water in Dish B evaporates in the same four hours. For this to be a fair test, the starting volume of water and the size and shape of the two dishes must be kept the same, so that only the amount of sunlight differs.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives the prediction, links more heat energy to a higher rate of evaporation, then names a control (same starting volume, same dish size), so it lands all three separately marked demands.
items.attentionCue: Underline every command in the stem before you write. Three instructions means three marks to chase, not one answer to polish.

items.stimulus:
Four identical wet cloths were left in different places. The time taken for each to dry completely was recorded.

Cloth W, shaded and still air: 300 minutes
Cloth X, shaded and windy: 180 minutes
Cloth Y, sunny and still air: 140 minutes
Cloth Z, sunny and windy: 80 minutes
items.stem: What can you infer about the conditions that affect how quickly water evaporates? Support each conclusion by naming the two cloths you compared and saying why that pair is a fair comparison.
items.whatItLooksLike: He scans the table, sees the sunny windy cloth dried fastest, and reports which conditions dried the cloths most quickly.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to state the conclusion each fair pair supports and to name the two cloths that differ by only one factor.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can move from the drying times to a general conclusion and justify it with a controlled comparison rather than the fastest row.
items.weakAnswer: Sunlight and wind both make water evaporate faster, because Cloth Z, which was sunny and windy, dried the fastest at 80 minutes.
items.thinkingGap: The conclusion is roughly right, but he reached it from the wrong place. Cloth Z dried fastest because two factors changed at once, so on its own it cannot show which factor did what, and that is exactly the trap the fourth row is built to catch. An infer question with data wants a controlled comparison: name two cloths that differ in only one condition (W and Y for sunlight, W and X for wind), then say what the difference in drying time proves. Quoting the fastest cloth is reading the table, not inferring from it, and two of the four marks live specifically in naming the fair pair and saying why it is fair.
items.strongAnswer: Comparing Cloth W with Cloth Y is a fair comparison because only the sunlight differs between them; the cloth in the sun dried faster, which shows that more heat energy increases the rate of evaporation. Comparing Cloth W with Cloth X is also fair because only the air movement differs; the windy cloth dried faster, which shows that moving air increases the rate of evaporation. Cloth Z cannot be used on its own for either conclusion, because both factors differ between it and Cloth W.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer pairs W with Y and W with X, shows each pair isolates a single variable, and reads the conclusion off that controlled difference, so it earns both the conclusion marks and the fair-comparison marks.
items.attentionCue: If you supported your conclusion with the fastest or biggest result, check whether more than one thing changed in it; real proof compares two rows that differ by ONE thing.

items.stem: Compare the properties of a liquid and a gas, and explain why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller container while a liquid cannot.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads 'why can a gas be squeezed' and pours everything he knows about gases onto the page.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to set liquid and gas side by side, a shared property and a differing one, then use the difference to explain the squeezing.
items.hiddenTest: Whether every point names both states, and whether he can apply the volume difference to the new situation of compression.
items.weakAnswer: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume, so it can spread out and fill its container, which is why it can be squeezed into a smaller space.
items.thinkingGap: Every word is true, but a compare question is marked on pairs, not on a solo portrait. He described the gas fully and left the liquid off the page entirely, so a marker cannot award the 'both have no definite shape' similarity or the 'a liquid has a definite volume, a gas does not' difference, because each of those marks needs both substances named in the same breath. 'Compare' is a signal that the answer must shuttle between the two things point by point. Describing one of them richly feels like effort, but it can only ever earn the marks that happen to mention the other by accident.
items.strongAnswer: Both a liquid and a gas have no definite shape, and both take the shape of the container they are in. However, a liquid has a definite volume while a gas has no definite volume. This means a gas spreads out and fills its container completely, whereas a liquid only occupies the lower part of the container. Because a gas has no definite volume, it can be squeezed into a container of smaller volume. A liquid has a definite volume that does not change, so it cannot be squeezed into a smaller space.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the shared property (neither has a definite shape) and the contrast (liquid has a definite volume, gas does not) with both named each time, then uses that contrast to explain why only the gas compresses, covering the similarity, the difference and the application.
items.attentionCue: Compare = every sentence mentions BOTH. If a marker can cross out one of the two things and your sentence still stands, it is not yet a comparison.

items.stimulus: A helium balloon is squeezed. Its shape changes, but the amount of gas inside stays the same.
items.stem: Explain why the gas inside the balloon can change shape when squeezed.
items.whatItLooksLike: He sees 'gas' and 'squeezed' and explains, correctly, why a gas can be compressed.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks specifically why the gas changes SHAPE, which is about a gas having no definite shape and taking the shape of its container.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he answers the exact property named in the question (shape) rather than the nearest familiar gas fact (compressibility).
items.weakAnswer: The gas can change because its particles are far apart and can be pushed closer together when the balloon is squeezed.
items.thinkingGap: This is true gas science, which is why it feels like a safe answer, but it answers a question that was not asked. 'Particles pushed closer together' explains why a gas can be compressed into a smaller volume; the stem asks why its SHAPE changes, which is a different property. The mark scheme wants two specific ideas: a gas has no definite shape, and it takes the shape of its container. He reached for the most familiar thing he knows about gases instead of the one the question named. Volume and shape are separate properties, and pattern-matching on the word 'squeezed' pulled him to the wrong one.
items.strongAnswer: A gas has no definite shape. It takes the shape of the container it is in. When the balloon is squeezed, the gas inside fills the new shape of the balloon, so its shape changes even though the amount of gas stays the same.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the exact property in the demand, that a gas has no definite shape and takes the shape of its container, and applies it to the balloon, so both marks are about shape, which is what was asked.
items.attentionCue: Answer the noun in the question, not the topic. 'Why does the SHAPE change' is not the same as 'why can a gas be squeezed'.

items.stimulus: A block of ice is taken from the freezer, left on a table until it melts, then heated in a pan until it boils away.
items.stem: Describe the changes of state that the water goes through, name each change, and explain why the temperature does not rise while the ice is melting.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'describe and name the changes of state' and produces a tidy narration from ice to steam.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the sequence of changes, the name of each, and, separately, the reason the temperature holds steady during melting.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he spots the 'explain why' buried at the end and can say the heat energy goes into changing state, not raising temperature.
items.weakAnswer: The ice gains heat and melts, changing from a solid to a liquid, and then the water boils, changing from a liquid to a gas.
items.thinkingGap: The description is accurate and correctly named, so it collects the describe marks and feels complete. But the stem quietly switches command word halfway through: after 'describe' and 'name' comes 'explain why the temperature does not rise while the ice is melting', and that is a reasoning demand carrying two or three of the five marks. He answered the part that suited a description and never noticed the part that asked for a cause. The hard, high-value idea, that the heat energy taken in during melting is used to change the state rather than to raise the temperature, is missing entirely, and it is the reason this question is worth five marks and not two.
items.strongAnswer: The ice gains heat energy from the surroundings and melts, changing from the solid state into the liquid state. While it is melting the temperature stays at its melting point, because the heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid rather than to raise the temperature. Once all the ice has melted, the heat energy gained raises the temperature of the liquid water. When the water reaches its boiling point it boils, changing from the liquid state into the gaseous state as water vapour.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer narrates and names both changes AND supplies the causal point that during melting the absorbed heat energy changes the state rather than raising the temperature, so it covers the description marks and the explanation marks the second command word demands.
items.attentionCue: When a stem changes command word midway ('describe ... and explain why ...'), it has become two questions. Answer both verbs.

items.stimulus: A neighbourhood has a problem with mosquitoes. Residents are asked to help reduce the mosquito population.
items.stem: Suggest one action residents could take, and explain how it would reduce the number of mosquitoes.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'name something that gets rid of mosquitoes' and offers the action he has heard before.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the action AND the mechanism: which stage of the life cycle the action attacks and why that reduces the number of adults.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can link removing stagnant water to the larval and pupal stages that depend on it, breaking the life cycle.
items.weakAnswer: Residents could remove any stagnant water and pour away water collecting in containers.
items.thinkingGap: The action is exactly the right one, so he feels he has answered, but 'suggest ... and explain how it would reduce the number' is two marks and he has only claimed the first. He named the what and skipped the why. The explanation mark lives in the mechanism: mosquitoes lay their eggs in stagnant water, and the larvae and pupae need that water to develop, so removing it breaks the life cycle before the adults can emerge. Without naming the stage the water supports, a correct action is just an instruction; the marker cannot tell whether he knows why it works.
items.strongAnswer: Residents could empty any containers holding stagnant water, such as flower pot trays. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in stagnant water, and the larvae and pupae need water to develop. Without stagnant water the eggs cannot hatch and develop, so the life cycle is broken and fewer adult mosquitoes are produced.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives the action and then traces the mechanism, that eggs and larvae need stagnant water so removing it stops them developing into adults, which is precisely the second, explanatory mark.
items.attentionCue: Suggest AND explain means the action is only half the marks. Always finish the sentence with 'which works because ...'.

items.stimulus: A farmer sprays a chemical on his crops that kills only the larvae of a particular moth. The adult moths are unharmed.
items.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of adult moths over the next few months and explain why. Suggest one reason why the number might not fall as much as expected.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads that the chemical kills the larvae and simply states that there will be fewer moths.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to predict the direction AND explain it through the life cycle, then give one reason the fall might be smaller than expected.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can supply the mechanism, that every adult must pass through the larval stage, rather than restating the premise as the conclusion.
items.weakAnswer: The number of adult moths will decrease over the next few months, because the chemical is killing off that kind of moth.
items.thinkingGap: The prediction direction is correct, but look at the 'reason': 'the chemical is killing off that moth' just says back what the stem already told him, dressed as an explanation. He has restated the premise, not explained it. The mark the examiner is guarding is the life-cycle link, that the chemical kills only the larvae, and since every adult must pass through the larval stage, fewer larvae must mean fewer adults. He also missed the final demand entirely: one reason the fall might be smaller, such as some larvae escaping the spray or adults flying in from unsprayed fields. A prediction only earns full marks when the reason adds something the question did not already give you.
items.strongAnswer: The number of adult moths will decrease. The chemical kills the larvae, so fewer larvae survive to develop into pupae and then into adult moths. Since the adult stage can only be reached by passing through the larval stage, fewer adults will be produced over the next few months. The number might not fall as much as expected because some larvae may not come into contact with the chemical and will survive, or adult moths may fly in from nearby fields that were not sprayed.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the decrease, explains it through the obligatory larval stage in the life cycle, and adds a limiting factor, so it satisfies the prediction, the mechanism and the 'why not as much' demands.
items.attentionCue: If your 'because' just repeats the situation you were given, you have not explained yet; add the step the question could not tell you.

items.stem: Compare the life cycle of a butterfly with the life cycle of a grasshopper, and explain why the young grasshopper competes with the adult for food while the young butterfly does not.
items.whatItLooksLike: He knows the butterfly life cycle cold, so he writes it out in loving detail and feels he has answered.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to hold the two life cycles side by side, then explain the consequence: why the grasshopper young competes with the adult and the butterfly young does not.
items.hiddenTest: Whether each point names both animals, and whether he reaches the competition-for-food reasoning, not just the stage differences.
items.weakAnswer: A butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis with four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The larva looks nothing like the adult and feeds on leaves, while the adult drinks nectar.
items.thinkingGap: It is accurate and well organised, but it is a portrait of one animal, not a comparison of two. The grasshopper, named twice in the stem, barely appears, so the marks for the shared feature (both start as an egg and undergo metamorphosis) and the contrast (complete versus incomplete metamorphosis, pupa versus nymph) cannot be awarded. Worse, he stopped at describing the stages and never reached the actual question: WHY the grasshopper nymph competes with its adult (same food, similar body) while the butterfly larva does not (different food from the adult). 'Compare ... and explain why' means the differences have to be put to work, not just listed for one side.
items.strongAnswer: Both the butterfly and the grasshopper begin life as an egg and both undergo metamorphosis. However, the butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis with four stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult, while the grasshopper undergoes incomplete metamorphosis with three stages, egg, nymph and adult. The grasshopper nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and has no wings, and it feeds on the same food as the adult, so the two stages compete with each other for the same food source. The butterfly larva looks completely different from the adult and feeds on leaves while the adult feeds on nectar, so the two stages do not compete.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the similarity and the difference with both animals in each point, then uses the nymph-resembles-adult versus larva-differs-from-adult contrast to explain the competition, which is where the final two marks sit.
items.attentionCue: Two named things in the stem means two named things in every point, and 'explain why' means the differences must lead somewhere.

items.stimulus:
Four sets of identical seeds were placed in different conditions for one week.

Set 1, moist cotton wool, warm, in light: germinated
Set 2, dry cotton wool, warm, in light: did not germinate
Set 3, moist cotton wool, warm, in darkness: germinated
Set 4, moist cotton wool, in a fridge, in light: did not germinate
items.stem: What can you infer about the conditions needed for germination? Support each conclusion by naming the two sets you compared.
items.whatItLooksLike: He knows what seeds need to germinate, so he writes the list down from memory.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to derive the conditions from THIS experiment and to prove each one by naming the two sets that differ by a single factor.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he reads the four sets as controlled comparisons rather than reciting textbook knowledge, and whether he catches that the data rules light out.
items.weakAnswer: Seeds need water, warmth and air to germinate, and they should be kept in good conditions.
items.thinkingGap: Every word could be true of seeds in general, and that is the problem: none of it is anchored to the experiment in front of him. An infer question is a reading task, not a recall task, and the marks are earned by naming Set 1 against Set 2 to prove water, and Set 1 against Set 4 to prove warmth, each pair differing by only one factor. Because he answered from memory, he also walked straight into the trap the data was built around: Set 3 germinated in darkness, which shows light is NOT needed, yet a remembered list happily includes conditions the experiment never tested. Support each conclusion by naming the sets, or the conclusion is just prior knowledge wearing the costume of an inference.
items.strongAnswer: Seeds need water and warmth for germination, but they do not need light. Comparing Set 1 with Set 2 is a fair comparison because only the water differs; only the moist set germinated, so water is needed. Comparing Set 1 with Set 4 is fair because only the temperature differs; only the warm set germinated, so warmth is needed. Set 3 was kept in darkness and still germinated, which shows that light is not needed. In each case only one factor was different between the two sets being compared, which is why each conclusion can be trusted.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer reads each conclusion off a single-variable pair (Sets 1 and 2 for water, Sets 1 and 4 for warmth) and uses Set 3 to rule light out, so every claim is tied to the specific data the question demands.
items.attentionCue: If your inference could have been written without ever looking at the table, you are reciting, not inferring; quote the two sets that prove it.

items.stimulus: A fruit is brightly coloured, sweet and fleshy, and contains hard seeds that are not digested by animals.
items.stem: Explain how the seeds of this fruit are dispersed.
items.whatItLooksLike: He matches 'sweet, fleshy fruit' to animal dispersal and writes the label.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks how the seeds are dispersed, the whole mechanism from the fruit being eaten to the seeds reaching new ground.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can carry the seed through the animal: eaten, not digested, passed out in droppings away from the parent plant.
items.weakAnswer: The seeds are dispersed by animals that come to eat the sweet, colourful fruit.
items.thinkingGap: Naming the agent, animals, is worth one mark, and the detail about the fruit being eaten is a good start, but at two marks the question wants the mechanism finished, and he stopped at the eating. The mark most often dropped here is the reason the seed survives the journey: the hard seeds are NOT digested, so they pass out unharmed in the animal's droppings at a spot away from the parent plant, where they can grow. 'Dispersed by animals' answers what carries the seed; it does not answer how the seed actually gets somewhere and stays alive, which is what 'how are the seeds dispersed' is really asking.
items.strongAnswer: The seeds are dispersed by animals. The bright colour and sweet, fleshy fruit attract animals to eat it. The hard seeds are not digested, so they pass out of the animal in its droppings at a place away from the parent plant, where they can germinate.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the agent and then completes the chain, attracted by colour and sweetness, eaten, seeds undigested, deposited in droppings away from the parent, so both the agent mark and the mechanism mark are secured.
items.attentionCue: 'How is it dispersed' wants the seed's whole journey, not just the vehicle. Follow it until it lands somewhere new.

items.stimulus: A student is asked to design a model seed that will travel as far as possible when dropped from a height in still air.
items.stem: Suggest two features the model seed should have and explain why each helps. Suggest one way the student could test fairly which of two model seeds travels further.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'design a seed that flies far', gives two clever features with reasons, and feels finished.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the two features AND a fair way to test which of two model seeds travels further, including what to keep the same and what to measure.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he notices the second, experimental half of the question and can state the control conditions and the measurement.
items.weakAnswer: The seed should have a large surface area so it catches the air and falls slowly, and a low mass so it is light and carried further.
items.thinkingGap: The two features and their reasons are exactly right and would earn two of the four marks, so the answer feels complete, but the stem has a whole second task after the design: 'suggest one way the student could test fairly which of two model seeds travels further'. That fair-test half is worth the other two marks, and he never started it. Design-and-test questions almost always split their marks evenly between the making and the testing, so a beautifully justified pair of features can still only score half. The missing marks want the controls named (same drop height, same air movement) and the measurement stated (horizontal distance travelled).
items.strongAnswer: The model seed should have a large surface area, for example papery wings or fine hairs, which increases the air resistance acting on it so that it falls more slowly and stays in the air longer. It should also have a low mass, because a lighter seed is more easily carried by moving air and so travels further. To compare two model seeds fairly, the student should release both from exactly the same height in the same room with the same air movement, and measure the horizontal distance each one lands from the release point.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives both features with air-resistance and mass reasoning, then describes releasing both seeds from the same height in the same conditions and measuring the distance travelled, so it claims the design marks and the fair-test marks.
items.attentionCue: A 'design a thing and test it' question pays half for the thing and half for the test. If you have not said what you would measure, you are only halfway.

items.stem: Describe what happens during pollination in a flowering plant, and state what must happen next before a seed can form.
items.whatItLooksLike: He reads it as 'describe pollination' and defines it neatly, the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to describe pollination AND to state the next event, fertilisation, that has to occur before a seed can form.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he knows pollination alone makes nothing, and can name fertilisation as the separate step that follows.
items.weakAnswer: During pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther of the flower to the stigma, carried by insects or the wind.
items.thinkingGap: This is a clean, correct description of pollination and earns those marks, which is why he moves on satisfied. But the stem has a second clause with its own mark: 'state what must happen next before a seed can form'. He treated the whole question as 'describe pollination' and let the tail of the sentence fall away. The idea being checked is that pollination on its own produces no seed; fertilisation must follow, with the pollen growing a tube to the ovule and the sex cells fusing. Naming pollination is only two-thirds of a three-mark question when the third mark is explicitly asking for the step after it.
items.strongAnswer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma. The pollen grains are carried there by an agent of pollination, such as an insect or the wind. Before a seed can form, fertilisation must follow: the pollen grain grows a tube down to the ovule, and the male sex cell fuses with the female sex cell inside it.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer describes the transfer from anther to stigma and its agent, then adds that fertilisation must follow before a seed forms, so it covers both the description and the crucial 'what happens next' mark.
items.attentionCue: '... and state what happens next' is a separate mark. When a stem points past the obvious answer, follow its finger.

items.stimulus: A farmer grows an orchard of fruit trees inside a large sealed greenhouse. No insects can enter, and there is no wind inside.
items.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of fruits produced and explain why. Suggest what the farmer could do to solve the problem without opening the greenhouse.
items.whatItLooksLike: He sees the sealed greenhouse with no insects and jumps straight to 'no bees, no fruit'.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to predict AND explain through the full chain, no agent so no pollination so no fertilisation so no fruit, and then suggest a fix.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can lay out the three separate causal links between 'no insects' and 'no fruit' rather than collapsing them into a single jump.
items.weakAnswer: There will be very few fruits, because there are no insects to pollinate the flowers. The farmer could put bees inside the greenhouse.
items.thinkingGap: The prediction is right and the fix is sensible, so this looks like a strong answer, but the explanation collapses three marks into one. 'No insects, so no fruit' skips the two links the examiner is actually paying for: no agent of pollination means pollen cannot be transferred from anther to stigma (no pollination), and without pollination there can be no fertilisation, and fruits form ONLY after fertilisation. He named the start and the end of the chain and left out the middle. A four-mark predict-and-explain wants each causal step written down, because the marks are hidden in the joins, not in the conclusion.
items.strongAnswer: Very few or no fruits will be produced. There are no insects and no moving air inside the sealed greenhouse to act as agents of pollination, so pollen grains cannot be transferred from the anther to the stigma. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot take place, and fruits only develop after fertilisation has occurred. To solve this without opening the greenhouse, the farmer could release insects such as bees inside it, or transfer the pollen himself from the anther to the stigma using a small brush.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer spells out every link, no agent, no transfer to the stigma, no fertilisation, no fruit, and then gives a workable fix, so it earns the prediction, all the mechanism marks and the solution mark.
items.attentionCue: When cause and effect sit far apart, write every stepping stone between them. Big jumps read as one mark, however right the landing.

items.stimulus:
Four identical flowering plants were treated differently and the number of fruits produced was counted.

Plant 1, left uncovered outdoors: 24 fruits
Plant 2, covered with a fine mesh bag: 2 fruits
Plant 3, covered with a fine mesh bag, pollen brushed onto stigmas by hand: 21 fruits
Plant 4, anthers removed and left uncovered: 19 fruits
items.stem: What can you infer from these results about how this plant is pollinated? Refer to each of the four plants in your answer.
items.whatItLooksLike: He walks through the table plant by plant, reporting how many fruits each one produced.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks him to conclude HOW the plant is pollinated, and to use each plant as evidence for that single conclusion.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can turn four fruit counts into one claim, that an outside agent carries pollen from another plant, with each plant supporting a step.
items.weakAnswer: Plant 1 made 24 fruits and Plant 2 made only 2. Plant 3 was bagged but hand-pollinated and made 21, and Plant 4 had its anthers removed but still made 19 fruits.
items.thinkingGap: He has read the table faithfully and copied out the evidence, but he has not inferred anything from it: every sentence he wrote was already printed in the question. An infer task wants the conclusion the numbers point to, that this plant needs an outside agent, most likely insects, to carry pollen to it from another plant. Each plant then becomes proof of a step: Plant 2 shows the bag blocks something needed, Plant 3 shows the missing something is pollen transfer to the stigma, and Plant 4 shows the pollen comes from a different plant because this one had no anthers. Restating the results is the raw material of an inference, not the inference. With five marks over four plants, the examiner is signalling that each row must do argumentative work, not just be reported.
items.strongAnswer: This plant relies on an outside agent, most likely insects, to carry pollen to it from another plant. Plant 1 was left uncovered and produced 24 fruits, which is the normal result. Plant 2 was bagged and produced almost none, showing that the bag blocked something the plant needs. Plant 3 was also bagged but had pollen brushed onto its stigmas by hand and produced 21 fruits, which shows that the missing step was the transfer of pollen to the stigma rather than anything else the bag prevented. Plant 4 had its anthers removed and still produced 19 fruits, which shows that the pollen must have come from a different plant.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the conclusion first, an external agent brings pollen from another plant, then makes each plant carry one link of that argument, which is how five marks across four rows are won.
items.attentionCue: If every sentence you wrote was already in the table, you have copied, not inferred. Say what the numbers PROVE, then let each row prove one part of it.

items.stimulus:
Four animals were examined and their characteristics recorded.

Animal W: body covered in scales, lays eggs on land, breathes with lungs
Animal X: body covered in feathers, lays eggs, breathes with lungs
Animal Y: moist skin, lays eggs in water, young breathe with gills and adults with lungs
Animal Z: body covered in hair, gives birth to young alive, breathes with lungs
items.stem: Infer which group each of the four animals belongs to, and state the characteristic you used for each.
items.whatItLooksLike: Copy out the interesting features of each animal from the table.
items.whatItsAsking: Decide the exact group each animal belongs to, and name the one characteristic that placed it there.
items.hiddenTest: Turning recorded observations into a classification: the group is the conclusion, the characteristic is only the evidence for it.
items.weakAnswer: Animal W has scales and lays its eggs on land. Animal X is covered in feathers. Animal Y has moist skin and its young breathe through gills. Animal Z has hair and gives birth to live young.
items.thinkingGap: Every line is true, but it is lifted straight off the table rather than worked out from it. To infer is to state the conclusion the evidence points to, and here that conclusion is the group: reptile, bird, amphibian, mammal. He has written down the clues and left out the answer they lead to, so the examiner sees an animal described but never placed. The characteristics are the evidence; the group name is the inference, and only the second is what this command word rewards.
items.strongAnswer: Animal W is a reptile, because its body is covered in scales and it lays eggs on land. Animal X is a bird, because its body is covered in feathers. Animal Y is an amphibian, because its young breathe using gills in water while the adults breathe using lungs on land. Animal Z is a mammal, because its body is covered in hair and it gives birth to its young alive.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names all four groups and hangs each on one deciding characteristic, so every sentence carries both the conclusion and the evidence that the four marks are split between.
items.attentionCue: Infer means commit to a verdict: name the group first, then the one feature that decided it, not just what the table already shows.

items.stem: Compare fungi with green plants.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what is special about fungi.
items.whatItsAsking: Give one way fungi and green plants are alike and one way they differ, naming both groups in each point.
items.hiddenTest: Whether a comparison holds two things side by side, rather than describing only the one that feels more interesting.
items.weakAnswer: Fungi do not have chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food by photosynthesis. Instead they get their food from dead and decaying matter.
items.thinkingGap: The science is right and even reaches for chlorophyll, but every clause is about fungi alone. A comparison needs both parties in the room: a difference only counts if it says what green plants do as well as what fungi do not. He has also skipped the similarity entirely, because he has read 'compare' as 'tell me about the odd one out'. Half a comparison, however accurate, is just a description of one side.
items.strongAnswer: Both fungi and green plants are living things which grow, reproduce and respond to their surroundings. However, green plants contain chlorophyll and can make their own food by photosynthesis, while fungi do not contain chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. Fungi instead obtain their food from dead or decaying matter.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer pairs a shared trait, both are living things that grow and reproduce, with a difference stated on both sides, plants have chlorophyll and photosynthesise while fungi do not and feed on decaying matter, which is exactly the similarity mark plus the difference mark.
items.attentionCue: Compare means both names in every point: not 'fungi cannot', but 'plants can, whereas fungi cannot'.

items.stimulus: A student places some bread in a sealed damp container and leaves it in a warm dark cupboard for one week.
items.stem: Predict what the student will observe on the bread after one week, and explain why.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what happens to old bread that is left lying around.
items.whatItsAsking: State that mould, a fungus, will grow, and give the conditions that let its spores grow.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can attach a cause to a predicted outcome, not just name the outcome anyone could guess.
items.weakAnswer: The bread will turn mouldy and go bad after a week.
items.thinkingGap: This is true, but it is the observation handed back, not an explanation of it. Warm, damp, dark bread going mouldy is exactly what the scenario sets up, so restating it earns almost nothing. The marks live one layer down: that the mould is a fungus, that its spores are already in the air, and that the warm, moist conditions plus the bread as food are what let those spores grow. 'It goes bad' names the result and stops at the very point where the question begins.
items.strongAnswer: Mould will grow on the bread. Mould is a fungus, and its spores are present in the air. The cupboard is warm, damp and dark, which are suitable conditions for the spores to grow, and the bread provides the food that the mould needs. The mould will therefore grow and spread across the bread.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names mould as a fungus and then supplies the mechanism, airborne spores landing and the warmth, moisture and food source enabling growth, which is the identification mark and the reasoning mark the two marks are for.
items.attentionCue: If your prediction is just the thing anyone would expect to see, you have described the outcome, not explained it: add the cause.

items.stimulus: The handle of a metal frying pan is made of plastic.
items.stem: Explain why the handle is made of plastic rather than metal.
items.whatItLooksLike: Name the property of plastic the question is fishing for.
items.whatItsAsking: Explain how that property protects the person holding the pan.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he carries a material property through to its consequence, instead of stopping at the technical term.
items.weakAnswer: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat.
items.thinkingGap: He has found the right keyword and stopped on it. 'Poor conductor of heat' is worth one mark, but the question asks why the handle is made of it, which needs the consequence: less heat is transferred through the plastic to the hand, so the handle stays cool enough to hold safely. Naming the property is not the same as explaining what it does. An explanation earns the second mark only when the term is followed through to its effect on the person.
items.strongAnswer: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat. This means heat energy from the hot pan is not easily transferred through the handle to the person holding it. Metal is a good conductor of heat, so a metal handle would become hot quickly and could burn the hand. The plastic handle therefore stays cool enough to hold safely.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the property and then completes the chain to the user, little heat transferred to the hand so it is safe to hold, which is the property mark and the consequence mark side by side.
items.attentionCue: Explain does not stop at the keyword: say what the property does and who it affects, then you have the second mark.

items.stimulus: A company wants to find out which of three fabrics is the most waterproof.
items.stem: Suggest how the company could test the three fabrics fairly, state what would be measured, and explain how they could make the result more reliable.
items.whatItLooksLike: Describe the general idea of testing the fabrics with water.
items.whatItsAsking: Give a controlled method with the variables kept the same, name the exact quantity measured, and add repeating for reliability.
items.hiddenTest: Whether a rough good idea can be sharpened into a fair, measurable and repeatable procedure.
items.weakAnswer: Pour some water onto each of the three fabrics and see which one lets the least water through. That fabric is the most waterproof.
items.thinkingGap: Nothing here is wrong, and it would even work in real life, which is exactly why it feels finished. But 'pour some water and see' names none of the things the four marks are counting: the same volume of water, the same height, area and time, which make it fair; the volume of water that passes through, which is the measurement; and repeating each test and averaging, which makes it reliable. A suggestion at this level is judged on its specifics, not its plausibility. The everyday version of a method scores the everyday number of marks, which is close to none.
items.strongAnswer: Stretch each fabric over the top of an identical container. Pour the same volume of water from the same height onto the same area of each fabric and leave each for the same length of time. Then measure the volume of water that has collected in each container; the fabric that lets through the least water is the most waterproof. Everything except the type of fabric must be kept the same so that the test is fair. To make the result more reliable, the company should repeat the test on each fabric several times and take the average volume, so that one unusual result does not mislead them.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer fixes every variable except the fabric, states the measured quantity as the volume of water passing through, and adds repeat and average, which lines up one to one with the four marks for fairness, measurement and reliability.
items.attentionCue: A method earns marks on its controls and its measurement, not on whether it would work: name what you keep the same, what you measure, and how many times.

items.stimulus: A student is given an unlabelled block and asked to find out whether it is made of a magnetic material.
items.stem: Describe a test the student could carry out, state what each possible result would show, and explain why this test cannot tell her whether the block is a magnet.
items.whatItLooksLike: Describe how to test the block with a magnet and read off the result.
items.whatItsAsking: Do that, and then explain the limitation: attraction cannot prove the block is itself a magnet.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he answers all three parts, including the reasoning about what the test cannot show.
items.weakAnswer: She should bring a magnet close to the block. If the block is attracted to the magnet, it is made of a magnetic material; if it is not attracted, it is not.
items.thinkingGap: The method is right and both outcomes are correct, so the first two parts are safely done. The trouble is the clause beginning 'explain why this test cannot tell her', which he has walked straight past. That third part is a separate demand and, by the mark scheme, the one that matters most: a magnet attracts both magnetic materials and other magnets, so attraction alone cannot show the block is a magnet, and only repulsion could. A three-part question is not finished just because two of its parts read well.
items.strongAnswer: The student should bring a magnet close to the block and observe what happens. If the block is attracted to the magnet, it is made of a magnetic material; if it is not attracted, it is not made of a magnetic material. However, this test cannot tell her whether the block is itself a magnet, because a magnet attracts both magnetic materials and other magnets. Only repulsion would show that the block is a magnet, since only two magnets can repel each other.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives the method, both results, and the limitation, that attraction cannot distinguish a magnet from a magnetic material since only two magnets repel, so it collects all three marks rather than the two on offer for the easy parts.
items.attentionCue: Count the verbs in the question and answer each one: describe, state and explain are three tasks, not one.

items.stimulus: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in the same bowl of hot soup. After two minutes, the handle of the metal spoon feels hot but the handle of the wooden spoon does not.
items.stem: Explain why the handle of the metal spoon feels hot, and explain why the wooden spoon's handle does not.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say why the metal handle gets hot. The metal spoon is the surprising one, so a rushing student treats it as the whole question.
items.whatItsAsking: Explain the metal handle AND the wooden handle. Two objects are named, so two explanations are owed, each anchored to how well that material conducts heat.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can carry the same idea, conduction, through to its opposite: a good conductor lets heat energy through quickly, a poor conductor does not.
items.weakAnswer: Metal is a good conductor of heat, so heat energy from the hot soup is conducted along the metal spoon to the handle. The handle gains heat energy, so it feels hot.
items.thinkingGap: Everything he wrote about the metal spoon is correct and would earn its marks. But the stem names two spoons and asks about both, and half the marks live in the wooden one. Because the metal spoon is the vivid, surprising case, he treats it as the entire question and never explains why wood, a poor conductor, keeps its handle cool. A complete comparison has to travel to the quiet side too.
items.strongAnswer: The soup is at a higher temperature than the spoon, so heat energy is transferred from the soup to the spoon. Metal is a good conductor of heat, so the heat energy is conducted quickly along the spoon to the handle. The handle gains heat energy and its temperature rises, so it feels hot. Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so very little heat energy is conducted along the wooden spoon, and its handle stays close to room temperature.
items.whyItWorks: It explains both spoons in the same frame: heat flows from the hotter soup, metal conducts it well so the handle heats up, wood conducts it poorly so the handle stays cool. Every object named in the stem gets its own sentence, so no mark is left behind.
items.attentionCue: If the question names two things, your answer has to visit both, even the boring one.

items.stimulus: A student builds a box to keep an ice cube from melting for as long as possible. Her first design is a thin cardboard box.
items.stem: Suggest one improvement to her design, explain how it would work, and explain why the phrase keeping the cold in is not a correct description.
items.whatItLooksLike: Suggest a better box and say why it works. A two-part suggest question, so the third instruction slips past unnoticed.
items.whatItsAsking: Three jobs: name an improvement, explain it using heat transfer, AND explain why saying the box keeps the cold in is the wrong way to describe what happens.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can not only use the correct heat-flow model but also spot and correct the everyday cold moves model when the question hands it to you.
items.weakAnswer: She could line the box with a thick layer of polystyrene, which is a poor conductor of heat. This slows down the heat energy passing from the warmer surroundings into the ice, so the ice gains heat more slowly and takes longer to melt.
items.thinkingGap: The insulation answer is genuinely good science and picks up two of the three marks. The trap is the third instruction, tucked at the end of the stem, to explain why keeping the cold in is wrong. Pleased with a clean insulation answer, he treats the question as finished and never states that cold is not a thing that moves, and that heat energy moves from the warm surroundings into the ice. The mark he missed was not hard; he simply stopped reading the question.
items.strongAnswer: She could line the box with a thick layer of a poor conductor of heat, such as polystyrene or wool. The surroundings are warmer than the ice, so heat energy is transferred from the surroundings to the ice; a poor conductor reduces the rate at which this happens, so the ice gains heat energy more slowly and takes longer to melt. Saying the box keeps the cold in is not correct, because cold is not a thing that can move. What actually happens is that heat energy moves from the warmer surroundings into the ice, and the insulation slows that down.
items.whyItWorks: It does all three jobs the stem set: a workable improvement, a mechanism built on heat moving from warm to cold, and an explicit correction of the cold in language by naming the real direction of heat flow. The last sentence earns the mark the examiner planted.
items.attentionCue: Count the instructions in the stem, then count the parts in your answer. The two numbers must match.

items.stimulus:
Three identical containers of hot water were each wrapped in a different material and their temperatures recorded every five minutes for thirty minutes.

Material D: fell from 80 to 74 degrees Celsius
Material E: fell from 80 to 58 degrees Celsius
Material F: fell from 80 to 45 degrees Celsius
items.stem: What can you infer about the three materials as conductors of heat?
items.whatItLooksLike: Read the numbers off and say which cooled the most and which cooled the least.
items.whatItsAsking: Turn the temperature drops into a conclusion about the materials as conductors of heat: rank them, and back the ranking with the size of each drop.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can move from what the data shows to what it means, using the idea that a smaller temperature drop means less heat energy was transferred to the surroundings.
items.weakAnswer: Material D only fell by 6 degrees Celsius, Material E fell by 22 degrees Celsius, and Material F fell by 35 degrees Celsius. So D lost the least heat and F lost the most.
items.thinkingGap: The figures are read off perfectly, and D lost the least, F lost the most is true. But an infer question is not asking what happened, it is asking what that tells you. He has handed back the evidence and stopped one step short of the conclusion the command word demands, that D is the poorest conductor of heat and F the best. The data is the support for the answer, not the answer itself.
items.strongAnswer: Material D is the poorest conductor of heat and Material F is the best conductor of the three. The water wrapped in D fell by only 6 degrees Celsius, showing that the least heat energy was transferred to the surroundings through it. The water wrapped in F fell by 35 degrees Celsius, showing that heat energy was transferred through it most quickly.
items.whyItWorks: It leads with the conclusion, D poorest and F best as conductors of heat, then uses the figures as evidence, linking the size of each temperature drop to how much heat energy was transferred. Conclusion first, data in support: that is what infer rewards.
items.attentionCue: If your sentence only says what the numbers are, you have described the data, not inferred from it. Infer asks: so what does it mean?

items.stimulus: A torch is shone at an opaque ball. A shadow of the ball appears on a screen behind it.
items.stem: Explain how the shadow is formed, and explain why the shadow has the same shape as the ball.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say that the ball blocks the light and makes a shadow behind it.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the mechanism: light travels in a straight line, the opaque ball blocks it, and because light cannot bend around the ball no light reaches the screen behind it, so the dark region takes the ball's outline.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you include the property that does the real work, that light travels in a straight line, which is the reason the light cannot simply go around the ball.
items.weakAnswer: The ball is opaque, so it blocks the light from the torch. No light can get through the ball, so a shadow is formed on the screen behind it, and the shadow is the same shape as the ball.
items.thinkingGap: Opaque and blocks are the right words, and nothing here is wrong. But the answer never says why the light cannot simply travel around the ball to fill in the shadow. The missing idea, that light travels in a straight line, is the whole mechanism; without it, blocks the light is a label rather than an explanation. It is also the phrase that separates an AL1 answer from an AL3 one here, and the reason the shadow matches the shape.
items.strongAnswer: Light from the torch travels in a straight line. The ball is opaque, so it does not allow light to pass through, and because light travels in straight lines it cannot bend around the ball. No light therefore reaches the part of the screen directly behind the ball, forming a shadow. The shadow has the same shape as the ball because the region of the screen that receives no light is bounded by the straight rays that just graze the edge of the ball, so it takes the outline of the object.
items.whyItWorks: It states the property that does the work, light travels in a straight line, then uses it twice: to explain why the opaque ball casts a shadow, and why that shadow takes the ball's shape. The mechanism, not just the keyword, is on the page.
items.attentionCue: Blocks the light names what happened. The mark is in why the light could not go around it.

items.stimulus: A student can see a red book on a table in a lit room. When the lights are switched off and the room is completely dark, she cannot see it at all.
items.stem: Explain why she cannot see the book in a completely dark room, and explain why she can see a lit torch bulb in the same dark room.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say she cannot see the book because the room is dark.
items.whatItsAsking: Explain seeing itself: the book is non-luminous, so we see it only by the light it reflects into our eyes, and in the dark there is none to reflect; the bulb is luminous, so its own light travels straight to her eyes.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can explain the mechanism of vision, reflected light entering the eye, rather than restate that darkness means no light.
items.weakAnswer: In a completely dark room there is no light, so she cannot see the book. But she can see the torch bulb because the bulb is switched on and gives out light.
items.thinkingGap: Both halves are true, and the bulb half is even nearly right. But no light, so she cannot see is the answer a young child would give; it never reaches the science the question is built on. The examiner wants the mechanism of seeing: a non-luminous book is visible only because it reflects light into the eye, so in the dark there is nothing to reflect. Staying at the general truth leaves the marks for non-luminous and reflects into the eyes untouched.
items.strongAnswer: The book is a non luminous object, which means it does not produce its own light. We are able to see it only because it reflects light from a source into our eyes. In a completely dark room there is no light for the book to reflect, so no light from the book enters her eyes and she cannot see it. A lit torch bulb is a luminous object: it produces its own light, which travels directly from the bulb into her eyes, so she can see it even when the room is dark.
items.whyItWorks: It replaces the general no light idea with the actual mechanism of vision: non-luminous objects are seen only by reflected light, so darkness leaves nothing to reflect, while a luminous bulb sends its own light to the eye. The precise terms carry the marks the general version missed.
items.attentionCue: If your explanation would satisfy a five year old, it is probably too general for the examiner. Name the mechanism.

items.stimulus: A student places a straight pencil into a glass of water and looks at it from the side.
items.stem: Describe what the student observes, and name the property of light that causes it.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what the pencil looks like in the water.
items.whatItsAsking: Two jobs: describe the observation precisely, that the pencil appears bent or broken at the surface though it is still straight, AND name the property of light behind it, that light changes direction passing from water to air.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you finish the question by naming the cause, and whether you say the pencil appears bent rather than is bent.
items.weakAnswer: The pencil looks bent or broken at the point where it enters the water, even though it is actually still straight.
items.thinkingGap: The description is genuinely good, careful even about appearance versus reality, and it banks the first mark. But the stem asks for two things joined by and: describe what is seen, and name the property of light that causes it. He did the describing and simply did not do the naming, so the second mark, for light changing direction as it passes from water into air, goes unclaimed. Half a question answered well is still half a question.
items.strongAnswer: The pencil appears bent or broken at the point where it enters the water, although it is still straight. This happens because light travelling from the pencil changes direction as it passes from the water into the air, so the part of the pencil below the surface appears to be in a different position from where it actually is.
items.whyItWorks: It delivers both halves: a precise observation that keeps appears and still straight, then the named cause, light changing direction as it moves from water to air. The and in the stem is answered on both sides.
items.attentionCue: When a stem is joined by and, it is two questions wearing one number. Answer both.

items.stem: Compare pitch and loudness of a sound.
items.whatItLooksLike: Explain the one you remember best, and hope it counts.
items.whatItsAsking: Hold pitch and loudness side by side: a shared basis, both are properties of sound produced by a vibrating source, then the difference, pitch depends on how fast it vibrates, loudness on how much energy the vibration carries.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can treat a comparison as one structure covering both terms, not a single term explained well.
items.weakAnswer: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. If an object vibrates faster the sound has a higher pitch, and if it vibrates more slowly the sound has a lower pitch.
items.thinkingGap: This is a strong paragraph about pitch, mechanism included, and had the question been explain pitch it would score well. But the command word is compare, and a comparison needs both terms in view: loudness never appears at all. Two of the three marks depend on loudness and on the shared idea that both arise from the vibrating source. Writing well about one half of a comparison does not cover the other half.
items.strongAnswer: Both pitch and loudness are properties of a sound and both depend on the vibration of the object producing it. However, pitch describes how high or low a sound is and depends on how fast the object vibrates, with faster vibration giving a higher pitch. Loudness describes how soft or loud a sound is and depends on how much energy the vibration carries, with more energy giving a louder sound.
items.whyItWorks: It opens with what pitch and loudness share, both properties of sound rooted in the vibrating source, then separates them cleanly: pitch by how fast it vibrates, loudness by how much energy the vibration carries. Both terms are present in every move, which is what compare means.
items.attentionCue: Compare means both words show up in your answer. If one of them is missing, you are only halfway there.

items.stimulus: A student strikes a drum and hears a sound from across the room.
items.stem: Explain how the sound reaches the student's ear, and state what would happen if the room were emptied of all air.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say the drum makes a sound and it travels through the air to her ear.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the mechanism from source to ear: the drum skin vibrates, the vibrations pass through the air, a medium, to the ear; then state that with no air there is no medium, so no sound is heard.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you treat sound as vibrations carried by a medium, rather than as a thing the drum sends out.
items.weakAnswer: When the drum is struck it makes a sound. The sound travels through the air across the room until it reaches the student's ear, so she hears it.
items.thinkingGap: It sounds complete, and travels through the air is even on the right track. But it never says the drum skin vibrates, or that sound is those vibrations being passed through the air. Sound is treated as a thing the drum produces and throws across the room, which is exactly the model the mark scheme is testing against. Naming sound and air is not the same as describing the vibration and the medium that carry it, and the answer also forgets the no-air case entirely.
items.strongAnswer: When the drum is struck, the drum skin vibrates. These vibrations are passed on to the air around the drum and travel through the air across the room to the student's ear, where they are detected and heard as sound. If the room were emptied of all air there would be no medium to carry the vibrations from the drum to the student, so no sound would be heard at all.
items.whyItWorks: It names the source as a vibration, the drum skin, follows those vibrations through the air, a medium, to the ear, and finishes the second half by ruling out sound in a vacuum because there is no medium. The mechanism, not just the words sound and air, is doing the explaining.
items.attentionCue: Sound is not sent, it is a vibration passed along. Name what vibrates and what carries it.

items.stimulus:
A student tapped one end of a long rod and measured how loud the sound was at the other end, using rods of the same size made of different materials.

Steel rod: very loud
Wooden rod: loud
Air column, no rod: faint
items.stem: What can you infer about how well sound travels through different materials? Support your answer with the results, and state which pair you compared.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say which rod carried the sound the loudest.
items.whatItsAsking: Infer the general pattern, sound travels better through solids than gases, support it with the results, and name the pair you compared to reach it.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can generalise from three named materials to the categories, solid versus gas, rather than just ranking the samples.
items.weakAnswer: The sound was very loud through the steel rod, loud through the wooden rod, and only faint through the air. So the steel rod let the sound travel through the best and the air was the worst.
items.thinkingGap: Reading the results and ranking them, steel best and air worst, is accurate, but it is still just the evidence. The question asks what you can infer, and the pattern the data supports is broader than steel: both solids, steel and wood, beat the gas, so sound travels better through solids than through gases. By staying with the three named samples he restates what the table shows, never reaches the category-level conclusion, and skips naming the pair he compared.
items.strongAnswer: Sound travels better through solids than through gases. Comparing the steel and wooden rods with the column of air, the sound was very loud through the steel rod and still loud through the wooden rod, both of which are solids, but only faint through the air, which is a gas. Because both solids carried the sound better than the gas did, the pattern is about the state of the material rather than about steel in particular.
items.whyItWorks: It gives the category conclusion, solids over gases, supports it with the loud-through-solids and faint-through-gas results, and names the pair compared. The ranking becomes evidence for a general claim instead of standing in for the answer.
items.attentionCue: Data gives you three samples; the inference is the rule behind them. Climb from steel is loudest to solids beat gases.

items.stem: Explain why the sun is described as the source of almost all the energy used by living things on Earth.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say that the sun gives energy to living things.
items.whatItsAsking: Trace the pathway: green plants convert the sun's light energy into stored energy in food by photosynthesis, and that energy passes to animals along the food chain.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you can supply the mechanism that makes the claim true, photosynthesis and the food chain, rather than repeat the claim in different words.
items.weakAnswer: The sun is the source of almost all the energy used by living things because the sun provides the energy that living things need to live and grow.
items.thinkingGap: This is the stem handed back with the words rearranged: the question already says the sun is the source, and the answer agrees that the sun provides the energy. Nothing has actually been explained. The marks are in the mechanism he skipped, that green plants convert light energy into stored energy in food through photosynthesis, and that this energy travels to animals along the food chain. An explanation has to add the how, not echo the claim.
items.strongAnswer: Green plants are producers. They absorb light energy from the sun and convert it into stored energy in the food they make during photosynthesis. When animals eat plants, this stored energy is transferred to them, and it passes further along the food chain when those animals are eaten. Almost all the energy used by living things can therefore be traced back to light energy from the sun.
items.whyItWorks: It supplies the pathway the claim rests on: plants convert the sun's light energy into food energy by photosynthesis, and the food chain carries that energy to animals. The word because is followed by a mechanism, not a paraphrase of the question.
items.attentionCue: If you could write your answer by shuffling the words of the question, you have not explained anything yet.

items.stimulus: Two identical balls are dropped onto the same hard floor. Ball A is dropped from 1 metre and Ball B from 2 metres.
items.stem: Predict which ball will bounce higher and explain why. Explain also why neither ball bounces back to the height it was dropped from.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say which ball bounces higher and why.
items.whatItsAsking: Two predictions to justify: which ball bounces higher, B, with more gravitational potential energy so more kinetic energy at impact, AND why neither returns to its starting height, because some energy is converted to heat and sound at the bounce.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you finish the question by explaining the energy lost at the bounce, using the sound of the bounce as the clue that energy has left the ball.
items.weakAnswer: Ball B will bounce higher. It is dropped from a greater height, so it has more gravitational potential energy at the start, and this is converted into more kinetic energy as it falls, so it hits the floor with more energy and bounces higher.
items.thinkingGap: The first half is excellent, gravitational potential energy converting to kinetic energy and more height meaning more energy at impact, and it earns every mark it targets. But the stem sets a second task with the word also: explain why neither ball returns to its full height. He stopped at the satisfying part and left the harder half, that some energy is converted into heat and sound at the bounce, unwritten. In a four mark question the unanswered half is where the grade is decided.
items.strongAnswer: Ball B will bounce higher. Because Ball B is released from a greater height it has more gravitational potential energy at the start, and as it falls this is converted into kinetic energy, so it strikes the floor with more energy and more is available to be converted back into gravitational potential energy as it rebounds. Neither ball returns to its starting height because at the moment of impact some of its energy is converted into heat energy and sound energy, which is why a bounce can be heard. That energy is no longer available to lift the ball, so each bounce is lower than the one before.
items.whyItWorks: It answers both instructions: which ball bounces higher, with the potential-to-kinetic reasoning, and why neither reaches full height, using the heat and sound produced at impact. The sound of the bounce, the examiner's planted clue, is turned into evidence that energy has left the ball.
items.attentionCue: The word also in a stem is a second question. And if you can hear it, feel it, or see it, energy has gone somewhere; say where.

items.stimulus: A toy car powered by a stretched rubber band travels only a short distance before stopping.
items.stem: Suggest one change that would make the car travel further, and explain why it would work.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say to stretch the band more so the car goes faster.
items.whatItsAsking: Suggest a workable change, stretch the band further, and explain it in energy terms: more elastic potential energy is stored, which is converted into more kinetic energy.
items.hiddenTest: Whether you name the energy store, elastic potential energy, and the conversion, rather than reaching for an everyday word like power or force.
items.weakAnswer: She could stretch the rubber band further before letting go. The more you stretch the band, the more power it has, so the car is pushed harder and travels a greater distance.
items.thinkingGap: The suggestion is right and would earn its mark, and stretch it further shows the idea is sound. But the band has more power uses a loose everyday word exactly where the mark scheme wants a named energy store and a conversion: stretching the band stores more elastic potential energy, which is converted into more kinetic energy. Power is not the quantity at work here, and the explanation mark is for the energy language, not the intuition.
items.strongAnswer: The rubber band could be stretched further before the car is released. Stretching it further stores a greater amount of elastic potential energy in the band. When the car is released, more elastic potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so the car moves off with more energy and travels a greater distance before friction converts all of that energy into heat energy and it stops.
items.whyItWorks: It keeps the sensible suggestion but explains it in the required terms: elastic potential energy stored by stretching, converted into kinetic energy on release, and finally into heat by friction. The energy store is named, so the explanation mark is earned.
items.attentionCue: When you feel yourself writing power or force, stop and name the energy: elastic, kinetic, heat.

items.stimulus: A ball is kicked straight up into the air. It slows down, stops for a moment, then falls back to the ground.
items.stem: Explain the motion of the ball using the forces acting on it, from the moment it leaves the foot until it lands.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say why the ball goes up and comes back down, and mention gravity.
items.whatItsAsking: Track the gravitational force through all three phases, rising, the instant at the top, and falling, and say what it does to the ball's speed in each.
items.hiddenTest: That the force never switches off. At the highest point the ball is momentarily still yet the gravitational force is still acting, which is the very reason it does not hang there.
items.weakAnswer: Gravitational force acts downwards on the ball. As it goes up, the force acts against its motion so it slows down. As it falls, the force acts in the same direction as its motion so it speeds up until it lands.
items.thinkingGap: Everything he has written is correct, and it reads like a finished answer, which is the trap. He has covered the rising and the falling, the two phases that feel obvious, and quietly skipped the moment at the top. That instant is a whole mark: the ball is stationary for a moment but the gravitational force is still pulling it down, which is the only reason it does not stay up there. Answering the easy two thirds of a four mark question feels complete but leaves a mark behind.
items.strongAnswer: Gravitational force acts on the ball throughout, pulling it downwards towards the Earth. As the ball moves upwards this force acts in the opposite direction to its motion, so the ball slows down. At its highest point the ball stops moving for an instant, but the gravitational force is still acting on it, which is why it does not stay there. As the ball falls, the gravitational force now acts in the same direction as its motion, so the ball speeds up until it lands.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer walks through all three phases and, crucially, says that at the highest point the ball stops for an instant while the gravitational force still acts on it. It earns the rising mark, the falling mark, and the top of flight mark that most answers miss, because it treats the force as continuous rather than as something that runs out.
items.attentionCue: When a stem says 'until it lands', account for every stage in between; the moment things seem to pause is usually where the hidden mark sits.

items.stimulus: A bicycle chain squeaks and the pedals are hard to turn.
items.stem: Suggest what could be done, and explain how it would help.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what to do about the squeaky, stiff chain.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the action, then explain it in force language: oiling reduces the frictional force between the moving surfaces.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can name the frictional force as the thing being reduced, instead of describing the everyday result of oiling.
items.weakAnswer: Put some oil on the chain so it runs smoothly and the pedals become easier to turn.
items.thinkingGap: He gets the action right and even states the outcome, so it feels answered. But 'runs smoothly' is an everyday description of the result, not the science that earns the second mark. The stem says 'explain how it would help', and the explanation wanted is that the oil forms a layer between the moving surfaces and reduces the frictional force between them. Naming the fix without naming the force is doing the deed but not the explaining.
items.strongAnswer: Oil should be applied to the chain. The oil forms a layer between the moving metal surfaces so that they do not rub directly against each other. This reduces the frictional force acting between them, so less force is needed to turn the pedals and the squeaking stops.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer applies oil and then says the oil separates the rubbing metal surfaces so the frictional force between them is reduced, which is why less force is needed to turn the pedals. The action scores one mark; the named, reduced frictional force scores the second.
items.attentionCue: 'Explain how it helps' on a forces question means name the force and say whether it goes up or down. 'Smoothly' is not a force.

items.stem: Compare frictional force and gravitational force.
