items.whatItLooksLike: Write what friction does, then write what gravity does.
items.whatItsAsking: Set the two forces side by side on the same points: one shared similarity, and a difference that names both forces in the same breath, contact versus no contact.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can hold both forces on one axis of comparison at once, especially the sharpest difference examiners reward: friction needs surfaces in contact, gravity needs none.
items.weakAnswer: Frictional force acts in the opposite direction to motion and slows a moving object down. Gravitational force pulls objects downwards towards the Earth.
items.thinkingGap: Both statements are true, and together they look like they cover both forces, so it feels like a comparison. But a comparison is not two separate descriptions parked next to each other; it is a single point that mentions both forces on the same feature. He has offered no similarity, and his 'difference' is really two facts that never meet. The mark scheme wants 'both can change an object's speed' as the similarity and 'friction needs contact while gravity needs none' as the difference, each point holding the two forces together.
items.strongAnswer: Both frictional force and gravitational force are forces that can change the speed of a moving object. However, frictional force acts only when two surfaces are in contact and moving against each other, and it always acts in the direction opposite to the motion. Gravitational force acts on an object without any contact being needed, and it always acts downwards towards the centre of the Earth.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer opens with a shared property, that both can change the speed of an object, then draws the difference on one axis: frictional force acts only when surfaces are in contact and opposes motion, whereas gravitational force needs no contact and always acts downwards. Every point names both forces, which is what turns description into comparison.
items.attentionCue: In a 'compare', every sentence should contain both things. If a sentence names only one, you are describing, not comparing.

items.stimulus: Two bar magnets are brought close together. In one arrangement they push apart. When one magnet is turned around, they pull together.
items.stem: Explain these two observations.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what happened when the magnets were pushed together and when one was turned around.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the rule behind each observation, like poles repel and unlike poles attract, matched to which arrangement caused which effect.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he moves from what he saw, push apart and pull together, to the pole rule that explains it, using the terms like and unlike poles.
items.weakAnswer: When the same ends face each other the magnets push apart, and when opposite ends face each other they pull together.
items.thinkingGap: What he wrote is accurate and correctly paired, but look closely: it says almost exactly what the stimulus already told him, only in his own words. 'Push apart' and 'pull together' are the observations, not the explanation. An 'explain' wants the underlying rule, that like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and the two marks are literally the words 'like poles' and 'unlike poles'. Rewording the question back is not the same as answering it.
items.strongAnswer: When the magnets pushed apart, like poles were facing each other, for example north facing north. Like poles repel each other, so the magnets were pushed apart. When one magnet was turned around, unlike poles faced each other, for example north facing south. Unlike poles attract each other, so the magnets were pulled together.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the arrangement, like poles facing such as north to north, then states the rule that like poles repel, and does the same for unlike poles attracting. It converts each observation into the scientific rule that produced it, which is exactly what the two marks reward.
items.attentionCue: If your explanation could have been written just by watching, without knowing any science, you have described, not explained.

items.stimulus:
Four objects were tested with a magnet and the results recorded.

Object P: strongly attracted
Object Q: not attracted
Object R: strongly attracted, and also repelled when turned around
Object S: not attracted
items.stem: Infer which object is a magnet and which are made of magnetic materials. Give your reasons, and explain why Object P cannot be a magnet.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what each object did in the test.
items.whatItsAsking: Turn each result into a labelled conclusion, which one is the magnet, which are magnetic materials, which are neither, and justify it with the rule that only a magnet can be repelled.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he uses repulsion as the single proof of a magnet, and can explain why attraction alone, as with Object P, is not enough.
items.weakAnswer: Object R was attracted and also repelled when it was turned around. Object P was strongly attracted but not repelled. Objects Q and S were not attracted at all.
items.thinkingGap: Every line is a faithful reading of the table, which is why it feels like the work is done. But the command word is 'infer', and inferring means stating the conclusion the evidence points to, not reciting the evidence. He has not said that R is the magnet, that P is a magnetic material, or that Q and S are neither, and he has not given the rule that only a magnet can be repelled. The observations are the raw material; the marks are for the labelled verdict and the reason.
items.strongAnswer: Object R is a magnet, because it was repelled by the magnet when turned around, and only another magnet can be repelled. Object P is made of a magnetic material but is not itself a magnet, because it was attracted but never repelled. Objects Q and S are not made of magnetic materials, because they were not attracted at all. P cannot be a magnet because if it were, turning it around would have brought like poles together and produced repulsion at some point during the test; since only attraction was ever observed, P must be a magnetic material rather than a magnet.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names R as the magnet because only a magnet can be repelled, names P as a magnetic material because it was attracted but never repelled, names Q and S as non magnetic, and explains that if P were a magnet, one orientation would have produced repulsion. Each conclusion is tied to the decisive evidence, which is what the four marks are for.
items.attentionCue: If a sentence could have been written just by reading the table, you have not inferred yet. Add the 'so this means'.

items.stimulus: A scrapyard needs to lift heavy pieces of iron and then release them into a container.
items.stem: Suggest why an electromagnet is more suitable than a permanent magnet for this job.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say why an electromagnet is good for lifting and then dropping the iron.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the electromagnet's useful property and say what the permanent magnet cannot do, because 'more suitable than' asks for a two sided answer.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he closes the comparison by contrasting with the permanent magnet, rather than only describing the electromagnet.
items.weakAnswer: An electromagnet is only magnetic while a current flows, so when you switch off the current it lets go of the iron and drops it into the container.
items.thinkingGap: This is a correct, well explained account of how the electromagnet does the job, so it looks complete. The catch is the phrase 'more suitable than a permanent magnet': the question is a comparison, and half of it is about the permanent magnet. He has explained why the electromagnet works but never said what the permanent magnet fails to do, that it cannot be switched off and so could never release the iron. The second mark lives on the side he did not write.
items.strongAnswer: An electromagnet is magnetic only while an electric current flows through its coil. When the current is switched off, the electromagnet loses its magnetism and the iron it was holding is released into the container. A permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so the iron would stay attached to it and could not be dropped where it is wanted.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the electromagnet's property, magnetic only while current flows so switching off releases the load, then contrasts directly: a permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so the iron would stay stuck. Naming both sides of 'more suitable than' secures both marks.
items.attentionCue: 'More suitable than X' is a comparison. You have to say something about X, not only about your choice.

items.stimulus: A food chain in a field is: grass leads to rabbit leads to fox. A disease suddenly kills most of the rabbits.
items.stem: Predict what will happen to the amount of grass and to the number of foxes, and explain why. Predict what will then happen to the rabbit population once the fox numbers have fallen.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what happens to the grass and the foxes after the rabbits die.
items.whatItsAsking: Predict the two immediate effects with reasons, then follow the chain one step further to the rabbits recovering once the foxes have fallen.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he can carry the chain past the first knock-on into the feedback loop: fewer foxes and plenty of grass let the surviving rabbits increase again.
items.weakAnswer: The amount of grass will increase because fewer rabbits are eating it. The number of foxes will decrease because rabbits are their main food source and there are far fewer to eat.
items.thinkingGap: The two predictions he gives are correct and even properly reasoned, so it feels like a finished four mark answer. But the stem asks a third thing outright, what happens to the rabbits once the foxes have fallen, and he has stopped at the immediate effects. Food chains push back in both directions: with fewer foxes hunting them and grass now plentiful, the surviving rabbits recover. That recovery is what separates a food chain from a list, and it is the mark he left behind.
items.strongAnswer: The amount of grass will increase, because there are far fewer rabbits left to feed on it. The number of foxes will decrease, because rabbits are the foxes' main food source and with far fewer rabbits many foxes will not obtain enough food to survive. Once the fox numbers have fallen, the surviving rabbits face less predation and have plenty of grass available, so the rabbit population will start to increase again.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives grass increasing and foxes decreasing with reasons, then completes the loop: with less predation and abundant grass, the rabbit population starts to rise again. It answers all three parts, so it collects the recovery mark that turns a correct but partial answer into a full one.
items.attentionCue: In a food chain question, read to the end of the stem. If it asks 'what happens next', the marks are in the knock-on, not the first effect.

items.stimulus: A food chain reads: lettuce, caterpillar, bird.
items.stem: Describe the role of each organism in this food chain.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what each organism does, who eats whom.
items.whatItsAsking: Name each organism's role using the technical terms: producer, consumer, and predator and prey.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he uses the vocabulary being tested, producer, consumer, predator, prey, rather than narrating the eating.
items.weakAnswer: The lettuce is eaten by the caterpillar, and the caterpillar is eaten by the bird.
items.thinkingGap: It is a true sentence, but it is the given food chain rewritten as a chain of who eats whom. The word 'role' asks for a label, not a narration: the lettuce is the producer because it makes its own food, the caterpillar and bird are consumers, and they are prey and predator. Describing the eating shows he follows the chain, but the two marks are specifically for the vocabulary, producer and consumer, that he never uses.
items.strongAnswer: The lettuce is the producer, because it makes its own food by photosynthesis. The caterpillar is a consumer, because it cannot make its own food and feeds on the lettuce; it is also the prey of the bird. The bird is also a consumer, and it is the predator that hunts and eats the caterpillar.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the lettuce as the producer that makes its own food, the caterpillar as a consumer and the bird's prey, and the bird as a consumer and the predator. It supplies the exact terms the question is testing, which is what 'describe the role' asks for.
items.attentionCue: When a question asks for a 'role', it wants the label. If you find yourself writing 'is eaten by', reach for the technical word instead.

items.stimulus: In a pond food web: algae are eaten by tadpoles and by small fish. Tadpoles are eaten by small fish and by dragonfly larvae. Small fish are eaten by herons.
items.stem: Infer what would happen to the number of herons if a chemical killed all the algae. Explain your reasoning.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what happens to the herons if the algae are killed.
items.whatItsAsking: State that the herons decrease, and trace the specific path: algae are the food source of tadpoles and small fish, those decline, and the herons that eat the small fish then decline too.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he fills in the middle of the chain, the organisms between algae and herons, rather than jumping from the cause straight to the final effect.
items.weakAnswer: The number of herons would decrease, because without the algae there would be less food in the pond for everything.
items.thinkingGap: He reaches the correct conclusion and even offers a reason, so it does not feel wrong, and it is not wrong, only vague. 'Less food for everything' is true of almost any food web disturbance; it does not show that he can read this particular web. The mark in the middle is for naming the link: algae feed the tadpoles and small fish, whose numbers fall, and herons eat the small fish. A reason general enough to fit any question usually earns the marks of none.
items.strongAnswer: The number of herons would decrease. Algae are the producer in this food web and are the food source for both the tadpoles and the small fish. If all the algae are killed, the tadpoles and small fish will have no food and their numbers will fall. Herons feed on the small fish, so with far fewer fish available the herons will not be able to obtain enough food and their number will decrease as well.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states that herons decrease, then traces the exact route: algae are the producer feeding tadpoles and small fish, which decline without them, and since herons feed on the small fish their numbers fall too. The specific middle step is the mark a general answer misses.
items.attentionCue: In a food web question, name the creatures in the middle. If your reason would fit any web, it is too general to score.

items.stimulus: A factory releases warm water into a river. Downstream, the number of fish falls sharply.
items.stem: Explain how the warm water could cause the number of fish to fall, and suggest one thing the factory could do to reduce the harm.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say why the warm water is bad for the fish, and how to reduce the harm.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the full mechanism, warm water holds less dissolved oxygen so the fish cannot get enough oxygen for respiration, plus a workable solution.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he inserts the dissolved oxygen step, the hidden link between 'warm' and 'fish die', instead of connecting them directly.
items.weakAnswer: The warm water raises the temperature of the river, and the fish cannot survive because it is too hot for them, so many die or move away. The factory could cool the water before releasing it.
items.thinkingGap: He has the cause, warm water and a higher temperature, the effect, fish dying, and a sensible solution, so three quarters of it looks solid. But the two middle marks are the mechanism he skipped: warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, and fish need that dissolved oxygen through their gills for respiration. 'Too hot for them' is a true sounding shortcut that hides the actual science. Without the oxygen step, the answer is only 'it got hot and they died', which is the observation, not the explanation.
items.strongAnswer: The warm water released by the factory raises the temperature of the river water. Warmer water is able to hold less dissolved oxygen than cooler water. The fish take in dissolved oxygen through their gills for respiration, so with less available they cannot obtain enough to survive, and many die or move away. To reduce the harm, the factory could cool the water down before releasing it into the river, or release it more slowly and in smaller amounts so that the river temperature rises far less.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer links the chain in full: the warm water raises the temperature, warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, the fish cannot obtain enough oxygen for respiration and so die or leave, and the factory could cool the water before releasing it. The dissolved oxygen step is worth two marks, and naming it is what makes this an explanation rather than a restatement.
items.attentionCue: When 'hot' leads to 'harm', ask what invisible step sits between them. Here it is the oxygen the warm water can no longer hold.

items.stimulus:
The number of a certain insect and the number of the birds that eat them were counted in a woodland over four years.

Year 1: 8000 insects, 120 birds
Year 2: 3000 insects, 130 birds
Year 3: 2000 insects, 70 birds
Year 4: 6000 insects, 50 birds
items.stem: What can you infer about the relationship between the insect and bird populations?
items.whatItLooksLike: Say how the insect and bird numbers changed over the four years.
items.whatItsAsking: State the relationship, the birds are predators and the insects their prey, and changes in the prey are followed by changes in the predators, supported with figures.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he states a predator and prey conclusion with the time lag, the predator responding after the prey, rather than describing the numbers going up and down.
items.weakAnswer: The insects went from 8000 down to 2000 by Year 3, and the birds changed too, dropping to 70 in Year 3 and 50 in Year 4 while the insects rose back to 6000.
items.thinkingGap: He has quoted the figures accurately, which feels like the hard part, but reading the table aloud is not inferring from it. 'Infer the relationship' wants the conclusion the numbers point to: the birds are the predators and the insects their prey, and the predator numbers change after the prey numbers, not alongside them. The figures are the evidence that supports that claim; on their own they are just the data he was given, rearranged. The marks are for the named relationship and the lag, quoted with figures, not for the figures alone.
items.strongAnswer: The birds are the predators and the insects are their prey, and each population affects the other. When the insect number fell from 8000 in Year 1 to 2000 in Year 3, the bird number then fell from 130 to 70, because there was less food available for the birds. In Year 4 there were only 50 birds, so fewer insects were eaten and the insect number rose again to 6000. Changes in the prey population are followed by changes in the predator population.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the predator and prey relationship, then shows the lag with figures: as the insects fell the birds fell after them because food was scarce, and in Year 4 the reduced birds let the insects recover. It pairs a conclusion with quoted evidence, which is the structure an 'infer from data' question rewards.
items.attentionCue: Quoting numbers is evidence, not an inference. Always finish with 'which shows that', then name the relationship.

items.stimulus: A river running through a town is polluted with rubbish and chemicals from nearby factories.
items.stem: Suggest one action that could reduce the pollution, and explain how it would help the living things in the river.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say one thing that would cut down the pollution.
items.whatItsAsking: Give the action and explain its effect on the living things: cleaner water lets the plants and animals survive and their numbers recover.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he completes the second half, the benefit to the organisms in the habitat, not just the action.
items.weakAnswer: The factories should treat their waste to remove the harmful chemicals before releasing it into the river.
items.thinkingGap: The action is practical and correct, so the answer feels done, but the stem asked for two things joined by 'and': the action, and how it would help the living things in the river. He has given only the first. A 'suggest' question about the environment almost always wants the consequence for the organisms: cleaner water means the plants and animals can survive and their numbers recover. Half the demand earns half the marks.
items.strongAnswer: Factories could be required to treat their waste to remove harmful chemicals before releasing it into the river. This would prevent harmful substances from entering the water, so the water quality would improve. The plants and animals living in the river would then be able to survive in their habitat, and their numbers could recover.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the action, treat the waste before release, then follows it to the living things: harmful substances no longer enter the water, the water quality improves, and the plants and animals can survive so their numbers recover. It answers both halves of the 'and', which is where the two marks sit.
items.attentionCue: When a stem says 'and explain how it helps the living things', the effect on the organisms is a separate mark. Never stop at the action.

items.stimulus: A desert plant has thick fleshy stems, and leaves that are reduced to thin spines.
items.stem: Explain how these two features help the plant survive in the desert.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what the thick stem and the spines are for.
items.whatItsAsking: For both features, give the function and link it to surviving in the desert: the stem stores water for the dry periods, the spines have a small surface area that reduces water loss.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he gives each of the two named features its own function and survival link, rather than developing one and merely mentioning the other.
items.weakAnswer: The thick fleshy stem stores water, which the plant can use during the long dry periods when there is no rain in the desert. It also has spines instead of ordinary leaves.
items.thinkingGap: The first feature is handled beautifully, feature, function, and survival in the desert all linked, which makes the answer feel strong. But the stem names two features and asks about both, and the spines are only mentioned, not explained. Naming a feature is not explaining it: the spines earn their marks by having a small surface area that reduces water loss. He did the harder half well and then let the second feature trail off, leaving its marks unclaimed.
items.strongAnswer: The thick fleshy stem stores water inside the plant. This allows the plant to survive during the long periods without rain in the desert, because it can use the stored water. The leaves are reduced to thin spines, which have a very small surface area. This greatly reduces the amount of water lost from the plant, so the plant conserves the water it has.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives each feature the full treatment: the fleshy stem stores water for the rainless periods, and the spines have a very small surface area that reduces water loss so the plant conserves what it has. Two features, two functions, both ending at survival in the desert, so every mark is accounted for.
items.attentionCue: If the stem names two features, each one needs its own function and its own link to survival. A feature merely mentioned scores nothing.

items.stimulus: An animal has the following features: a thick layer of fat under its skin, a dense white coat, and broad feet with fur on the soles.
items.stem: Infer the habitat this animal is adapted to live in, and explain how each feature helps it.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say where the animal lives and what its features do.
items.whatItsAsking: Name the cold, snowy habitat and give each feature a precise function: the fat and coat insulate to reduce heat loss, the white coat camouflages against snow, the broad feet spread the weight.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he uses precise adaptation language, insulate and reduce heat loss, rather than the loose 'keeps it warm', and ties each feature to the specific habitat.
items.weakAnswer: The animal lives somewhere very cold. The thick fat keeps it warm, the white coat helps it hide, and the big feet help it walk on the snow.
items.thinkingGap: He identifies the habitat and pairs each feature with a benefit, so it reads as a complete answer, and none of it is false. The problem is precision: 'keeps it warm' misses the actual mechanism, that the fat insulates the body and reduces heat loss to the cold surroundings. The fat does not make heat, it slows its escape, and the examiner looks for the word 'insulate' or the phrase 'reduce heat loss'. Loose, everyday phrasing carries the right idea without saying the thing that scores.
items.strongAnswer: The animal is adapted to live in a very cold, snowy habitat. The thick layer of fat and the dense coat both insulate its body, reducing the loss of heat energy to the cold surroundings so that it stays warm. The white coat camouflages it against the snow, making it harder for predators or prey to see it. Its broad feet spread its weight over a larger surface area so it does not sink into the snow.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the cold, snowy habitat and then sharpens each function: the fat and dense coat insulate and reduce heat loss, the white coat camouflages against the snow, the broad feet spread the weight over a larger surface area. Precise verbs turn a general description into four scoring points.
items.attentionCue: 'Keeps it warm' is everyday; 'insulates and reduces heat loss' is the mark. For each feature, reach for the exact scientific verb.

items.stimulus: A water lily has broad flat leaves that float on the surface. A cactus has leaves reduced to spines.
items.stem: Compare how the leaves of these two plants are adapted to their habitats.
items.whatItLooksLike: Say what the water lily's leaves do, then what the cactus's leaves do.
items.whatItsAsking: Compare the two on one shared idea, surface area, with a similarity and a difference that names both plants: large surface area to absorb sunlight versus small surface area to reduce water loss.
items.hiddenTest: Whether he compares on the shared axis of surface area, holding both plants in each point, rather than describing each leaf separately.
items.weakAnswer: The water lily has broad flat leaves that absorb a lot of sunlight for photosynthesis. The cactus has spines that cut down the water it loses.
items.thinkingGap: Both halves are correct and each names a real advantage, so it looks like a comparison of the two plants. But the sentences run on separate tracks: one is about sunlight, the other about water, and they never meet on a common idea. The link the examiner wants is surface area, the water lily's large surface area absorbs more sunlight while the cactus's small surface area reduces water loss, plus the similarity that both leaves are adapted to their habitat. Two accurate descriptions side by side are not yet a comparison.
items.strongAnswer: Both plants have leaves that are adapted to help them survive in their own habitat. However, the water lily has broad flat leaves with a large surface area, which absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis and float on the surface where water is plentiful. The cactus has leaves reduced to spines with a very small surface area, which greatly reduces the water lost from the plant, because water is scarce in the desert.
items.whyItWorks: The strong answer states the similarity, that both leaves are adapted to their habitat, then contrasts on one axis: the water lily's large surface area absorbs more sunlight where water is plentiful, while the cactus's small surface area reduces water loss where water is scarce. Surface area runs through both halves, which is what makes it a comparison worth three marks.
items.attentionCue: A comparison needs a shared idea running through both things. Find the one word, here surface area, that both halves turn on.

items.stimulus:
Four materials were each placed in a gap in a circuit containing a bulb, and what happened was recorded.

Material 1: bulb lit brightly
Material 2: bulb did not light
Material 3: bulb lit brightly
Material 4: bulb did not light
items.stem: Infer which materials are conductors of electricity and which are insulators. Explain how you decided.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it just wants you to sort the four materials into two lists depending on whether the bulb lit.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks you to name each material as a conductor or an insulator and to say what the lit or unlit bulb proves about the current and the circuit.
items.hiddenTest: Turning an observation from a results table into a labelled conclusion with its reasoning.
items.weakAnswer: Materials 1 and 3 lit the bulb and Materials 2 and 4 did not. So 1 and 3 let the electricity through.
items.thinkingGap: Every word of that is correct, but the examiner wrote the bulb behaviour into the question, so repeating it earns nothing. Inference marks are paid for the conclusion the data forces, not the data itself: that a lit bulb means current flowed and the circuit was complete, so the material is a conductor. The student stopped at what he could see and never named what it means.
items.strongAnswer: Materials 1 and 3 are conductors of electricity. When they were placed in the gap the bulb lit, which shows that current was able to flow through them and complete the circuit. Materials 2 and 4 are insulators. The bulb did not light with them in the gap, which shows that they did not allow current to flow, so the circuit remained incomplete.
items.whyItWorks: It names all four materials for the first two marks, and it converts the lit bulb into its meaning, current flowed and the circuit was completed, which is the third and most-missed mark.
items.attentionCue: If your sentence could have been written just by looking at the picture, you have not inferred yet.

items.stimulus: Two bulbs, A and B, are connected in a series circuit with one battery. Bulb A is removed from its holder, and bulb B goes out.
items.stem: Explain why bulb B goes out when bulb A is removed, and state what would happen instead if the two bulbs were connected in parallel.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like a single question about why bulb B goes out in a series circuit.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for two things: why the break stops bulb B in series, and what parallel would do differently.
items.hiddenTest: Reading a stem that hides a second task behind the word and, and showing the path idea works in both arrangements.
items.weakAnswer: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current, so when bulb A is removed there is a gap and the circuit is broken. No current can flow, so bulb B goes out.
items.thinkingGap: This is a clean, correct, mark-worthy answer to the first half, and that is exactly the danger. The stem asks him to state what would happen instead if the two bulbs were connected in parallel, and that clause carries its own mark. A strong first half makes a student feel finished, so the eye slides past the second instruction. Two-thirds of a perfect answer is still only two-thirds of the marks.
items.strongAnswer: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current to flow around. When bulb A is removed there is a gap in that path, so the circuit is broken and no current can flow through bulb B, which therefore goes out. If the two bulbs were connected in parallel, each would be on its own separate path from the battery. Removing bulb A would break only its own path, leaving the path through bulb B complete, so bulb B would stay lit.
items.whyItWorks: It earns the series marks (one path, break stops the current through B), then answers the parallel clause the stem demanded, showing the path idea was understood rather than memorised for one case.
items.attentionCue: Circle every and in the stem: each one is usually a second mark waiting to be forgotten.

items.stem: Compare a series circuit and a parallel circuit, and explain which arrangement is used for the lights in a house and why.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to describe what a parallel circuit is and why it is the good one for a house.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks you to set the two circuits side by side, a shared feature and a difference stated in terms of both, then let the house example follow from that difference.
items.hiddenTest: Whether a comparison names both things in the same breath, rather than describing one and leaving the other implied.
items.weakAnswer: In a parallel circuit each bulb is on its own separate path, so if one bulb blows the others stay lit. That is why houses use parallel circuits.
items.thinkingGap: Everything said about parallel is true, and the house conclusion is right, yet a comparison question is only half-built when only one side is described. The command word compare requires series to appear in the same sentences as parallel: one path versus separate paths, a break stopping everything versus a break stopping one branch. Describing parallel alone leaves the examiner to supply the contrast, and the marks for the contrast go unclaimed.
items.strongAnswer: Both a series circuit and a parallel circuit are complete circuits in which current flows from the source through the components. However, a series circuit has only one path for the current, so all the components are on the same path, while a parallel circuit has separate paths for each component. As a result, a break anywhere in a series circuit stops the current everywhere, but a break in one branch of a parallel circuit leaves the other branches working. The lights in a house are connected in parallel, so that when one lamp blows the rest stay lit and each can be switched on and off on its own.
items.whyItWorks: It gives the similarity (both complete circuits), the difference stated for both (one path versus separate paths), the consequence for both (break stops all versus one branch), and lets the household choice fall out of that consequence, hitting all four marks.
items.attentionCue: Compare means both names in every sentence: if one circuit is missing, so is the mark.

items.stem: Describe the path taken by a piece of bread through the digestive system, naming what happens at each main stage, and state what happens to the parts of the bread the body cannot digest.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants the order of the organs the bread passes through.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks what happens to the bread at each stage, an event per organ, plus the fate of what cannot be digested.
items.hiddenTest: Whether a describe-the-pathway answer supplies the action at each stage or just the itinerary.
items.weakAnswer: The bread goes into the mouth, then down the gullet to the stomach, then the small intestine, then the large intestine, and the rest comes out as faeces.
items.thinkingGap: The organs are correct and in the right order, so it feels like a full answer, but naming the stops on a route is not describing the journey. Five marks signals five distinct events, and this sentence contains almost none: no chewing and saliva, no churning, no absorption into the bloodstream, no water reabsorbed. Listing where the bread goes without saying what is done to it at each place typically scores about one of the five.
items.strongAnswer: In the mouth the bread is chewed into smaller pieces and mixed with saliva, which begins the digestion of starch. It then passes down the gullet into the stomach, where it is churned and digested further. It moves into the small intestine, where digestion is completed and the digested food is absorbed into the bloodstream. The parts of the bread the body cannot digest pass into the large intestine, where water is absorbed from them, and the remaining material is then removed from the body as faeces.
items.whyItWorks: It pairs each organ with its event, chewing and saliva, churning, absorption into the blood, water reabsorbed, removal, giving five separate scoring points instead of one list.
items.attentionCue: The mark is in the verb, not the organ: at every stage, say what is done to the food.

items.stimulus:
Samples were taken from different parts of a person's digestive system two hours after a starchy meal, and tested for starch.

Mouth: starch present
Stomach: some starch present
Start of small intestine: trace of starch
End of small intestine: no starch
items.stem: What can you infer from these results about the digestion of starch?
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to notice that the starch reading gets smaller and disappears by the end.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks what that falling reading means: that starch is being broken down as it travels, and that its digestion is completed in the small intestine.
items.hiddenTest: Reading a downward trend as a process, and knowing starch is broken down rather than simply vanishing.
items.weakAnswer: There is less and less starch along the digestive system, and by the end of the small intestine there is no starch left.
items.thinkingGap: The trend is described accurately, but the table already shows the readings falling; the examiner can see that. The inference is what the falling numbers prove: the starch is being digested, broken down into smaller substances, and that process is finished by the end of the small intestine. Saying the starch disappeared or is gone also quietly dodges the science, because starch cannot simply leave; it has to be broken down, and naming that is the whole point.
items.strongAnswer: The starch is gradually digested as the food travels through the digestive system. The amount of starch decreases from the mouth to the stomach and then to the start of the small intestine, and no starch remains at the end of the small intestine. This shows that starch is broken down into smaller substances along the way, and that its digestion is completed in the small intestine.
items.whyItWorks: It states the conclusion (starch is progressively broken down) and locates where digestion finishes (the small intestine), the two marks, using the falling readings as support rather than as the answer.
items.attentionCue: A trend in the table is the evidence; the mark is for what the trend proves.

items.stimulus: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered with millions of tiny finger like projections.
items.stem: Explain how these projections help the small intestine to carry out its function.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants the fact that the projections increase the surface area.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the surface area point and then what that larger surface area is for: absorbing more digested food into the bloodstream.
items.hiddenTest: Completing a structure-to-function chain, not stopping at the structure's property.
items.weakAnswer: The tiny projections increase the surface area of the inner wall of the small intestine.
items.thinkingGap: This is the sentence that feels like the answer, because surface area is the term everyone is chasing, but it is only the first half of the chain. The question asks how the projections help the intestine do its job, and its job is absorption; a larger surface area is worth stating only once it is connected to more digested food being absorbed into the bloodstream. The student named the mechanism and stopped one clause short of the function it serves.
items.strongAnswer: The tiny finger like projections greatly increase the surface area of the inner wall of the small intestine. A larger surface area means that more digested food can come into contact with the wall at one time, so more digested food can be absorbed into the bloodstream in the same period. This makes absorption faster and more efficient.
items.whyItWorks: It gives both halves the two marks require: the projections increase surface area, and that larger surface area lets more digested food be absorbed into the bloodstream.
items.attentionCue: Larger surface area is never the finish line: always add for what.

items.stem: Describe what happens in the chest during inhalation, and explain why the air flows in rather than being sucked in.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the diaphragm and ribs move and the chest gets bigger so air comes in.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the full chain, diaphragm and ribs, volume up, pressure down, then air flowing from higher pressure outside to lower pressure inside.
items.hiddenTest: Carrying a description all the way to the pressure difference that actually drives the air in.
items.weakAnswer: The diaphragm contracts and moves down, the rib muscles pull the ribcage up and out, and the chest gets bigger, so air flows into the lungs.
items.thinkingGap: The moving parts are named correctly and the chest does enlarge, so it reads like a competent answer, but it stops at the halfway house. It never reaches why enlarging the chest moves any air: the volume increase lowers the air pressure inside the lungs below the pressure outside, and air flows from high pressure to low. Without the pressure step the answer has described the machinery but not the cause, and the clause about air not being sucked in is left unanswered.
items.strongAnswer: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and moves downwards, while the rib muscles contract to pull the ribcage upwards and outwards. These movements increase the volume of the chest cavity. As the volume increases, the air pressure inside the lungs decreases until it is lower than the air pressure outside the body. Air always flows from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure, so air flows in through the nose and windpipe into the lungs. It is not sucked in; it is pushed in by the higher pressure outside.
items.whyItWorks: It lays down all five events, diaphragm down, ribcage up and out, volume up, pressure down, air flows high to low, which also answers the not-sucked-in clause the stem planted.
items.attentionCue: Movements change volume, volume changes pressure, pressure moves the air: never stop before pressure.

items.stimulus: The lungs contain millions of tiny air sacs, each surrounded by very fine blood vessels.
items.stem: Explain how this structure helps gaseous exchange to take place efficiently.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the air sacs give a big surface area so oxygen gets into the blood.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks how the structure speeds gaseous exchange in both directions: oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of it.
items.hiddenTest: Remembering that gaseous exchange is two gases moving opposite ways, not just oxygen entering.
items.weakAnswer: The millions of air sacs give a large surface area, so a lot of oxygen can pass into the blood quickly.
items.thinkingGap: The surface area point is right and oxygen does pass in, but gaseous exchange is a two-way traffic and only one direction has been described. Carbon dioxide passing from the blood into the air sacs to be breathed out is the other half of the exchange, and the mark scheme expects both gases named, moving in opposite directions. An answer that follows only the oxygen has described half the process and earns half the marks.
items.strongAnswer: The millions of tiny air sacs give the lungs a very large total surface area for gaseous exchange. Each air sac is surrounded by very fine blood vessels, so the gases only have to travel a very short distance between the air and the blood. Oxygen can therefore pass from the air in the sacs into the bloodstream, and carbon dioxide can pass from the blood into the air sacs, both very quickly and in large amounts.
items.whyItWorks: It gives the large surface area for gaseous exchange and then names both gases moving in opposite directions, which is the completeness the two marks reward.
items.attentionCue: Gaseous exchange is a two-way street: name the gas going out as well as the one coming in.

items.stimulus: Smoking damages the walls of the air sacs in the lungs, causing many of them to break down and join into fewer, larger spaces.
items.stem: Predict how this would affect the person, and explain why.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the damaged lungs make the person breathless.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the effect and the reason: fewer, larger spaces mean a smaller surface area, so less oxygen enters the blood.
items.hiddenTest: Supplying the mechanism behind a predicted symptom, not just the symptom.
items.weakAnswer: The person will get breathless easily and will not be able to exercise like they used to, because their lungs have been damaged by smoking.
items.thinkingGap: The prediction is right and breathless is even the word the mark scheme wants, but because their lungs are damaged just restates the stem, which already told him the air sacs broke down. Two of the three marks live in the mechanism the student skipped over: fewer, larger spaces give a much smaller surface area for gaseous exchange, so less oxygen passes into the bloodstream with each breath. A prediction is only worth its full marks when the why does work the question has not already done.
items.strongAnswer: The person will become breathless easily and will not be able to exercise as they did before. When the air sacs break down into fewer, larger spaces, the total surface area available for gaseous exchange is greatly reduced. Less oxygen can therefore pass from the lungs into the bloodstream with each breath, so the body cannot obtain enough oxygen for respiration, especially when the demand rises during exercise.
items.whyItWorks: It keeps the correct prediction, then supplies the two mechanism marks the restatement missed: reduced surface area, so less oxygen enters the blood per breath.
items.attentionCue: If your because only repeats the question, the reason mark is still unclaimed.

items.stimulus:
Blood samples were taken from three blood vessels and the amount of oxygen in each was measured.

Vessel X: high oxygen, leaving the lungs
Vessel Y: low oxygen, entering the lungs
Vessel Z: low oxygen, leaving a leg muscle
items.stem: Infer why Vessel Z contains blood with a low amount of oxygen. Explain your reasoning.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to note that Vessel Z is leaving the muscle and has low oxygen.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks why the oxygen is low: the muscle cells absorbed the oxygen from the blood and used it in respiration to release energy.
items.hiddenTest: Explaining a low reading through the process that caused it, rather than repeating the reading.
items.weakAnswer: Vessel Z has low oxygen because it is the blood leaving the leg muscle, and the muscle used up the oxygen.
items.thinkingGap: The first clause reads the table straight back, and the muscle used up the oxygen is true but stays at the surface. The inference the marks want is the mechanism underneath: oxygen passed from the blood into the muscle cells, which used it in respiration to release the energy the muscle needs to work. Used up names the outcome without the process, so the blood leaving is deoxygenated for a reason the answer never quite states.
items.strongAnswer: Vessel Z carries blood away from the leg muscle. As the blood passed through the muscle, oxygen passed from the blood into the muscle cells. The muscle cells used this oxygen in respiration to release the energy needed for the muscle to work. The blood leaving the muscle is therefore deoxygenated and contains a low amount of oxygen.
items.whyItWorks: It replaces used up with the two scoring ideas: oxygen passed into the muscle cells, and it was used in respiration to release energy.
items.attentionCue: Used up is a description; name the process, respiration for energy, to make it an inference.

items.stimulus: A student's heart rate is 72 beats per minute at rest and 145 beats per minute during exercise.
items.stem: Explain why the heart rate increases during exercise.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the muscles need more oxygen so the heart beats faster.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks what the faster-flowing blood is delivering and removing, and why it is needed more quickly during exercise.
items.hiddenTest: Building the full supply-and-demand chain rather than stopping at more oxygen.
items.weakAnswer: During exercise the muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to pump blood around the body more quickly.
items.thinkingGap: Oxygen is the right keyword and the answer is genuinely true, but it stops at the first link and leaves the chain unfinished. The mark scheme wants the muscles' need spelled out, more oxygen and digested food for respiration to release more energy, and it wants the return trip, the extra carbon dioxide carried away faster. Naming oxygen alone, without respiration, energy, or the waste being removed, gives the idea but not the mechanism the two marks are paying for.
items.strongAnswer: During exercise the muscles are working harder and need more energy, which is released during respiration. Respiration requires oxygen and digested food, so the muscles need these to be delivered more quickly. The heart therefore beats faster to pump blood around the body more rapidly, so that more oxygen and digested food reach the muscles and the carbon dioxide produced is carried away more quickly.
items.whyItWorks: It reaches both marks: the muscles need oxygen and digested food for respiration to release energy, and a faster heart rate delivers these and removes carbon dioxide more quickly.
items.attentionCue: Do not stop at oxygen: say what it is for, respiration and energy, and what leaves as well.

items.stimulus: A doctor advises a patient to exercise regularly to improve the health of the heart.
items.stem: Suggest how regular exercise benefits the circulatory system, and explain why.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to agree that exercise is good for the heart.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for a specific benefit and its mechanism: the heart is a muscle, so exercise strengthens it and it pumps more blood per beat.
items.hiddenTest: Turning a general health claim into the muscle mechanism that earns the mark.
items.weakAnswer: Regular exercise is good for you and keeps the heart healthy, so the circulatory system works better.
items.thinkingGap: Nothing here is wrong, which is exactly why it scores nothing: it is a true statement that could be written about almost any organ without knowing a thing about the heart. The mark depends on one specific idea, that the heart is a muscle, and like any muscle it grows stronger when it is worked, so a stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat. A general good for you floats above the scenario; the mark sits in the mechanism it skips.
items.strongAnswer: Regular exercise makes the heart stronger. The heart is a muscle, and like any other muscle it becomes stronger when it is worked regularly. A stronger heart can pump a larger volume of blood with each beat, so oxygen and digested food are delivered to the body more efficiently and the resting heart rate can be lower.
items.whyItWorks: It supplies the two marks a good-for-you answer misses: the heart is a muscle that strengthens with use, and a stronger heart pumps blood more efficiently.
items.attentionCue: If your answer would fit any topic, it fits none: name the mechanism only this scenario has.

items.stimulus: Plant A is left on a sunny windowsill. Plant B is placed in a dark cupboard. Both are watered equally. After three days Plant A has grown taller than Plant B.
items.stem: Explain why Plant A grew taller than Plant B. Explain also why Plant B did not die immediately even though it could not make food.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say Plant A grew more because it got sunlight to photosynthesise.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the photosynthesis mechanism, sunlight makes food for growth, and then why Plant B survived a while: it lived on stored food.
items.hiddenTest: Naming what photosynthesis produces and using it, plus answering the survival clause.
items.weakAnswer: Plant A grew taller because it was in the sunlight, so it could carry out photosynthesis. Plant B was in the dark and could not photosynthesise.
items.thinkingGap: Photosynthesis is the word the question is built around, so producing it feels like scoring, but the naming is not the mechanism. The chain has to close: photosynthesis uses sunlight to make food, and that food is what the plant uses to grow, which is why the lit plant grew taller. And the second instruction, why Plant B did not die at once, is untouched; its two marks live in the stored food idea, that Plant B lived off food made earlier and would only die once that store ran out. The keyword was there; the reasoning and the second half were not.
items.strongAnswer: Plant A received sunlight, so it was able to carry out photosynthesis, using the sunlight absorbed by the chlorophyll in its leaves to make food, which it used to grow. Plant B was kept in the dark, so it could not photosynthesise and could not make any new food, and therefore could not grow as tall. Plant B did not die immediately because it still had food stored in its leaves and stem from before it was placed in the dark, and it used that stored food to stay alive. It would only die once that store ran out.
items.whyItWorks: It turns the keyword into a mechanism, photosynthesis makes food used for growth, and then answers the survival clause with the stored-food idea, covering all four marks.
items.attentionCue: Naming photosynthesis is not explaining it: say it makes food, and say what the food is for.

items.stimulus:
Four identical potted plants were kept for a week and then their leaves tested for starch.

Plant 1, in sunlight, watered, normal air: starch present
Plant 2, in darkness, watered, normal air: no starch
Plant 3, in sunlight, watered, air with carbon dioxide removed: no starch
Plant 4, in sunlight, not watered, normal air: no starch
items.stem: What can you infer from these results? Explain how the data supports each conclusion.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to notice that only Plant 1 made starch and the other three did not.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks you to conclude that sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are each needed for photosynthesis, and to prove each with the pair of plants that differ by only that one factor.
items.hiddenTest: Attaching each conclusion to its own fair comparison, not just reporting which plants had starch.
items.weakAnswer: Plant 1 made starch but Plants 2, 3 and 4 did not. So the plant needs sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make starch.
items.thinkingGap: The reading of the table is correct and the final list is even the right answer, but the marks are not in the list, they are in the matching. Each factor has to be pinned to the pair that isolates it: Plant 1 against Plant 2 for light, against Plant 3 for carbon dioxide, against Plant 4 for water, each pair differing in one thing only. Reporting which plants had starch, then jumping to it needs all three, shows the destination without the reasoning that gets you there, and an unsupported conclusion of this kind earns about one mark of four.
items.strongAnswer: Sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are all needed for photosynthesis. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 2, where only the light differed, only the plant in sunlight produced starch, so sunlight is needed. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 3, where only the carbon dioxide differed, only the plant supplied with carbon dioxide produced starch, so carbon dioxide is needed. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 4, where only the water differed, only the watered plant produced starch, so water is needed.
items.whyItWorks: It states each conclusion beside its own named, fair pair, which is exactly the one-mark-per-comparison structure the four marks are built on.
items.attentionCue: One conclusion needs one fair pair: prove each factor with the two plants that differ by only that factor.

items.stem: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in a green plant, and explain why a plant kept in complete darkness for many days will eventually die.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to explain what photosynthesis is and then say the plant dies without light.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks you to hold the two processes side by side, what each uses and makes and when each happens, then use that to explain the death in darkness.
items.hiddenTest: Whether both processes are contrasted in the same breath, and whether respiration is known to run at all times.
items.weakAnswer: Photosynthesis makes food using carbon dioxide, water and sunlight, and releases oxygen. Without any light the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it cannot make food and it dies.
items.thinkingGap: Photosynthesis is described accurately, but a comparison needs respiration standing next to it, and here respiration barely appears. The marks want both processes set against each other: photosynthesis makes food and releases oxygen, respiration breaks food down to release energy and releases carbon dioxide, and crucially photosynthesis needs light while respiration runs at all times. That last point is what makes the death explainable: in darkness the plant keeps respiring and using food but makes none, so the store runs out. Describing only photosynthesis leaves the contrast, and the reason for death, half-formed.
items.strongAnswer: Both photosynthesis and respiration take place inside the cells of a green plant, and both involve oxygen and carbon dioxide. However, photosynthesis makes food using carbon dioxide, water and sunlight and releases oxygen, while respiration breaks down food to release energy, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis takes place only when there is light, whereas respiration takes place at all times, day and night. A plant kept in complete darkness will eventually die because it continues to respire and so keeps using up food, but with no light it cannot photosynthesise to make any more. Once its stored food is exhausted it can no longer release the energy it needs to stay alive.
items.whyItWorks: It gives the similarity, both processes for both, and the timing contrast, then lets the death follow from respiration continuing while photosynthesis stops, covering all five marks.
items.attentionCue: Compare two processes by naming both each time: a paragraph about one is not a comparison.

items.stem: Compare the sperm cell and the egg cell.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the sperm is small with a tail and swims to the egg.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for what the two cells share and how they differ, each difference stated for both cells, with the reason behind the size.
items.hiddenTest: Framing every point as a contrast of both cells, and giving the reason for a difference rather than the difference alone.
items.weakAnswer: The sperm cell is small and has a tail so it can swim towards the egg.
items.thinkingGap: This is a true and even useful fact, but it is a description of the sperm, not a comparison, and the egg is missing from every clause. A comparison names both cells together: both are sex cells with a nucleus that fuses at fertilisation; the sperm has a tail to swim while the egg cannot move; the egg is far larger because it carries a store of food for the embryo. Note too that the egg is big on its own is a weak difference; the mark is for why it is big. One cell described is at most one side of a three-mark contrast.
items.strongAnswer: Both the sperm cell and the egg cell are sex cells, and both contain a nucleus which fuses with the other at fertilisation. However, the sperm cell has a tail which allows it to swim towards the egg, while the egg cell has no tail and cannot move by itself. The egg cell is also much larger than the sperm cell, because it contains a store of food to nourish the embryo after fertilisation.
items.whyItWorks: It states the shared feature and two differences, each in terms of both cells, and gives the reason for the size difference, matching the three marks.
items.attentionCue: A comparison mentions both cells in every point: describing one is only half the contrast.

items.stimulus: A developing baby in the uterus is connected to the mother by the umbilical cord.
items.stem: Explain the function of the umbilical cord, and explain why the developing baby cannot obtain oxygen and food for itself.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the cord carries food and oxygen from the mother to the baby.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the cord's full two-way job and, separately, why the baby cannot get oxygen and food on its own.
items.hiddenTest: Covering both directions of transport and answering the second clause about why the baby is dependent.
items.weakAnswer: The umbilical cord carries oxygen and digested food from the mother's blood to the developing baby, which it needs to grow.
items.thinkingGap: This correctly describes the supply half, and it is worth a mark, but traffic along the cord runs both ways and the return half is missing: waste, including carbon dioxide, is carried from the baby back to the mother to be removed. The stem then adds a second question, why the baby cannot obtain oxygen and food for itself, and that has been ignored altogether; its marks lie in the baby being surrounded by fluid, unable to breathe air or eat, so everything must come from the mother. A confident first clause hides two whole marks that were never attempted.
items.strongAnswer: The umbilical cord carries oxygen and digested food from the mother's blood to the developing baby, which the baby needs for respiration and growth. It also carries waste substances, including carbon dioxide, away from the baby to the mother so that she can remove them. The baby cannot obtain these for itself because it is surrounded by fluid inside the uterus, so it cannot breathe air into its lungs and it cannot take in or digest food. Everything it needs must therefore be supplied through the umbilical cord.
items.whyItWorks: It gives both directions of transport (supply in, waste out) and answers the dependency clause (surrounded by fluid, cannot breathe or eat), reaching all four marks.
items.attentionCue: A cord carries both ways and a stem with two explains has two answers: check you gave both.

items.stimulus:
The mass of a developing baby was recorded during pregnancy.

End of month 3: 25 g
End of month 5: 300 g
End of month 7: 1200 g
End of month 9: 3400 g
items.stem: What can you infer about the growth of the baby during pregnancy?
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the baby grows and gets heavier during pregnancy.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks what pattern the numbers reveal: not only that the baby grows, but that the rate of growth increases as pregnancy goes on.
items.hiddenTest: Reading a table for the shape of the change, the accelerating rate, not just the direction.
items.weakAnswer: The baby grows during the pregnancy, and its mass increases from 25 g to 3400 g.
items.thinkingGap: That the baby grows is true and the figures are quoted, but it gets heavier is what anyone sees at a glance, and the table was given precisely so more could be drawn from it. The inference worth the extra marks is the rate: the gain is 275 g between months 3 and 5 but 2200 g between months 7 and 9, so growth speeds up as pregnancy progresses, which is why the baby needs an increasing supply of nutrients. Reporting the rise without noticing its shape uses the table as a picture rather than as data.
items.strongAnswer: The baby grows throughout the pregnancy, with its mass increasing from 25 g at the end of month 3 to 3400 g at the end of month 9. The rate of growth also increases as the pregnancy progresses: the mass increased by 275 g between months 3 and 5, but by 2200 g between months 7 and 9. This means the baby needs an increasing supply of nutrients from the mother as the pregnancy continues.
items.whyItWorks: It states the direction and then the deeper conclusion, an increasing rate, supported by comparing the gains in two periods, which is the three-mark structure.
items.attentionCue: It gets bigger is the glance; the mark is for the pattern in how fast it changes.

items.stimulus: A ring of bark, containing the food carrying tubes, is removed from all the way around the trunk of a tree. The water carrying tubes deeper inside are left undamaged.
items.stem: Predict what will happen to the roots of the tree, and explain why.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say the tree, or its roots, will die after the bark is cut.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the outcome and the reason: food made in the leaves can no longer travel down the cut food-carrying tubes to reach the roots.
items.hiddenTest: Explaining a prediction through the specific tube system that was cut, and knowing the two tube systems do different jobs.
items.weakAnswer: The roots will eventually die because the ring of bark was removed from all the way around the trunk.
items.thinkingGap: The prediction is correct, but the because simply feeds the stem back: the question already said the ring was removed, so repeating it explains nothing. The reasoning the marks want runs through the food-carrying tubes in the bark: food made in the leaves is transported down through them, and cutting a complete ring severs that route so no food can pass below the cut to the roots. It matters that the water-carrying tubes are untouched, so the leaves still get water; it is the downward food supply that fails, and naming that is where the marks are.
items.strongAnswer: The roots will not receive any food and will eventually die. Food made in the leaves during photosynthesis is transported to the rest of the plant through the food carrying tubes in the bark. Removing a complete ring of bark cuts these tubes all the way around the trunk, so food from the leaves can no longer be carried down past the cut to the roots. Without a supply of food the roots cannot survive.
items.whyItWorks: It keeps the prediction and adds the mechanism the restatement skipped: food travels down the food-carrying tubes, the ring cuts them all round, so no food reaches the roots.
items.attentionCue: If the because just repeats the stem, you have restated, not explained.

items.stem: Explain why water is important to a plant, giving three separate uses, and state which of them stops first when the plant is not watered.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to explain that a plant needs water to live and grow.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for three distinct jobs water does in the plant, plus which one fails first when water runs short.
items.hiddenTest: Producing several specific, separate uses instead of one general statement, and linking the science to the visible symptom.
items.weakAnswer: Water is very important to a plant because a plant needs water to survive and grow, and without it the plant will die.
items.thinkingGap: It is perfectly true that a plant needs water to live, and perfectly useless as an answer, because it is one vague idea where the question asked for three specific ones. The marks are itemised: water is a raw material for photosynthesis, water keeps the cells firm to support the plant, and water carries dissolved mineral salts around it. A fourth mark asks which fails first, support, which is why wilting is the earliest sign. Needs water to survive collapses all of that into a generality that fits every plant and scores like a single point.
items.strongAnswer: Water is one of the raw materials the plant needs for photosynthesis, in which it makes its food. Water inside the cells also keeps them firm, which supports the plant and keeps the stem and leaves upright. In addition, the mineral salts absorbed from the soil are dissolved in water and transported in it to all parts of the plant. When a plant is not watered, the support function fails first: the cells lose water and are no longer firm enough to hold the leaves up, which is why wilting is the earliest visible sign that a plant needs water.
items.whyItWorks: It supplies three separate, named uses, one mark each, plus the fourth for identifying support as the first to fail and tying it to wilting.
items.attentionCue: Three uses means three different sentences: a single needs-it-to-live is one vague mark at best.

items.stem: Describe the path taken by water from the soil to a leaf of a plant, and explain what makes the water move upwards.
items.whatItLooksLike: It looks like it wants you to say water goes from the roots up the stem to the leaves.
items.whatItsAsking: It asks for the labelled path, root hairs, water-carrying tubes, stem, leaves, and the force that drives it up: transpiration pulling water behind it.
items.hiddenTest: Naming the specific structures on the route and supplying the mechanism that lifts the water without a pump.
items.weakAnswer: The water is taken in by the roots and travels up the stem to the leaves of the plant.
items.thinkingGap: The route is broadly right, so it reads as an answer, but it is too coarse for four marks and the mechanism is missing entirely. The path should be named at each stage: absorbed from the soil by the root hairs, into the water-carrying tubes, up through the stem to the leaves. And the final mark is the driving force: a plant has no pump, so water lost from the leaves by transpiration pulls the water below it upwards. Travels up the stem states that it rises without saying what lifts it, which is the very thing the second half of the stem asked for.
items.strongAnswer: Water in the soil is absorbed by the root hairs of the plant and passes into the water carrying tubes inside the root. From there it travels upwards through the water carrying tubes in the stem and into the leaves. The water moves upwards because water is continually being lost from the leaves as water vapour by transpiration. As water leaves the top of the tubes, it pulls the water below it upwards, drawing a continuous column of water up from the roots.
items.whyItWorks: It names each structure on the path, root hairs, water-carrying tubes, stem, leaves, and supplies the transpiration-pull mechanism, which is the fourth and most-missed mark.
items.attentionCue: It goes up is not a mechanism: with no pump, name what pulls the water, transpiration.
